Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.
The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.

“Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: trust vs vigilance by reader group and AI type

blocks.x: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. The authors tested this in the diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency, with a multi-reader crossover study of 1,750 interpretation events: clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model.

High AI reliability paradoxically induced automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. When challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists showed a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors; given the small specialist cohort, the authors call this hypothesis-generating.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: reader performance unaided, with reliable AI and with error-injected AI

blocks.x: They argue clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s resilience to algorithmic failure rather than standalone accuracy, and release an open-source educational sandbox to inoculate clinicians against automated errors and mitigate deskilling.

In a routine prenatal ultrasound, possible fetal brain abnormalities are flagged for MRI, but imperfect imaging can lead to missed or incorrect diagnoses. Researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital and Inria have developed a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion, capturing a high-resolution image for the radiologist. The work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision.

When the head shifts during a scan, each 2D slice can be taken from a different angle, leaving coverage gaps. Rather than learning physics from data, E(3)-Pose embeds the left-right symmetry of the fetal head in its architecture, making it easier to identify the brain’s orientation.

blocks.cap: An MRI scan of a fetal brain (outlined in yellow) in the sagittal position.

blocks.x: Boston Children’s Ellen Grant says the work “will automate fetal brain MRI,” bringing faster, more comfortable scans and higher-quality images. First author Ramya Muthukrishnan now hopes to extend the model, trained mainly on third-trimester fetuses, to younger ones: “the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.”

Medical AI (CEO Kwon Joon-myung), a company specializing in medical artificial intelligence (AI), said on the 15th that its heart failure diagnostic aid medical device software 'AiTiALVSD' had obtained 510(k) Clearance (premarket clearance) from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

blocks.cap: Photo courtesy of Medical AI

blocks.x: 'AiTiALVSD' is software that uses AI to analyze electrocardiogram data routinely measured in hospitals and help diagnose left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), a type of heart failure. This is the first time a Korean company has cleared the U.S. FDA bar with software offering this function.

Heart failure outcomes can improve greatly when it is detected early, but because early symptoms are often unclear, patients frequently do not go on to echocardiography and miss the window for treatment. 'AiTiALVSD' acts as an ECG-based digital biomarker, with AI detecting subtle ECG changes that are hard for the human eye to catch.

The clearance follows a multi-ethnic, multi-setting clinical trial of more than 20,000 (2만 명) patients at 6 major U.S. hospitals that verified consistent accuracy. In a blinded head-to-head validation study by Amsterdam University Medical Center in the Netherlands, recently presented at the European Society of Cardiology, it also recorded the highest accuracy, ahead of leading ECG AI models.

There are about 6.7 million (670만 명) heart failure patients in the U.S. Having secured U.S. approval following Europe, the United Kingdom, India and Singapore, Medical AI plans to expand its U.S. business in earnest in cooperation with local medical institutions and partners.
CEO Kwon Joon-myung said, "Now that we have completed preparations to enter the U.S., the largest market in the world, we will work to achieve strong results."

The Ministry of Health and Welfare and the World Health Organization (WHO) have set out joint international principles to guarantee clinician oversight and final human judgment when AI is used in health care, and to spread AI technologies whose clinical effectiveness and safety have been verified.

blocks.cap: Minister of Health and Welfare Jeong Eun-kyeong (left) and WHO Director-General Tedros (right) at a press briefing. Photo by reporter Lee Jae-won

blocks.x: Minister Jeong and Director-General Tedros jointly announced the 'AI Healthcare Seoul Declaration for Responsible Innovation and Global Solidarity' at the opening ceremony of the '2026 World Bio Summit' on the 21st. It is the first joint declaration on health AI issued by the ministry and the WHO Director-General.

The declaration sets out the principle that AI should be used within its validated scope, under conditions that allow human oversight, and that final judgment rests with humans. It also recommends governance proportionate to the level of risk, from development through use.

It also includes principles on preventing data monopolies and market dominance, harmonizing international standards and regulation, supporting the participation of low- and middle-income countries, and managing biosecurity risks. "This does not mean innovation can proceed without safeguards," Director-General Tedros said.

Minister Jeong said the ministry is in working-level talks with WHO on building a global AI hub, and that it will demonstrate and validate AI technologies before expanding them to low- and middle-income countries.
Lung puncture biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing lung nodules, but poor CBCT image quality and limited guidance intelligence slow procedures, particularly for small and complex lesions.

Researchers led by Huazhong University of Science and Technology built GPS-Lung, a Generative AI-Powered Puncture Surgery Navigation System, and tested it in a multicenter randomized controlled trial (NCT06762613).

With GPS-Lung, surgeons needed fewer punctures (2.0 ± 1.2 vs. 2.5 ± 1.7, P = 0.005), operative time fell from 23.2 ± 6.3 to 20.4 ± 5.6 minutes (P = 0.001), and radiation exposure dropped from 5570.9 to 4357.4 μGy·m² (P = 0.033).
Pneumothorax complications fell from 23.9% to 12.7% (P = 0.033). The authors say the system made the procedure more standardized and efficient.
Avenda Health is launching Surgery Mode, a suite of intraoperative features for its Unfold AI prostate cancer mapping platform.
The platform analyzes a patient's MRI, biopsy, pathology, and prostate-specific antigen data to produce a 3D map of the cancer's extent.

Surgery Mode allows surgeons to use the maps during robotic and nonrobotic procedures. New capabilities include enlarged 3D views and a cancer estimation map that can be adjusted to match the surgical console's camera angle; review of underlying MRI slices during the procedure; a capsule risk score overlay that automatically mirrors the surgical camera view, providing color-coded risk by quadrant to guide nerve-sparing decisions; and updated case management and administrative tools for physicians and staff.
Unfold AI predicts cancer spread into nearby anatomy with 92% accuracy, compared with 52% using MRI alone, according to the company.
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, yet the real-world performance of FDA-cleared AI detection models remains incompletely characterized.

Emory University researchers retrospectively evaluated two FDA-cleared Aidoc BriefCase algorithms across a 17-facility academic health system: one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE on routine contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 37,191). Reference labels came from radiology reports via a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, κ = 0.94).

The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity. Sensitivity fell from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE. The incidental-PE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity.

Both models showed lower sensitivity than their FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, which the authors say underscores the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.

An AI tool may be able to help doctors judge how ill a patient is using a single photograph of their face, say US researchers. Trained on millions of healthy faces and 35,000 photos of cancer patients, it estimates survival by looking closely at features near the eyes. The preliminary findings are published in the Lancet Digital Health.

blocks.cap: Facial regions most important to cancer survival (left) and to age (right). Mass General Brigham/Lancet Digital Health

blocks.x: The 'FaceSurvival' tool points to the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose as most vital, across many cancer types, including ones that had spread to bone or brain. A second tool, 'FaceAge', estimates biological age from areas such as the nasolabial folds, forehead and temples.

Lead researcher Dr Raymond Mak of Mass General Brigham says the goal is to make face-based health assessment "more quantitative, consistent and scalable" to support treatment decisions "rather than replace physician judgment". The team says it needs far more data, especially from different ethnic groups.
Prof Miroslaw Bober of the University of Surrey calls it "a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use", warning: "Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it."
Not-for-profit health system Sentara Health deployed a new artificial intelligence case management solution Tuesday, which it co-developed with clinical decision support company Regard.
Case managers can use the tool to query charts in plain language, quickly surfacing key insights like patient history and status changes, and can view changes within the last 24 hours.

“It's incredible to think about how much time we used to spend piecing together a patient's story before they could even start discharge planning,” said Rollin Reeder, M.D., Sentara's chief health information officer.

Sentara plans to expand the tool across acute care and into ambulatory care. Executives say it could save nearly 90,000 hours, equivalent to more than 40 full-time employees and nearly $5 million in labor costs. Sentara operates 12 hospitals and more than 400 care sites in Virginia and Northeast North Carolina.
Regard CEO Eli Ben-Joseph said its platform has surfaced more than 20 million diagnoses that physicians accepted, and extending it to operational teams is “a natural next step.”

‘Opportunistic Screening,’ which uses a CT taken to check for a specific condition to also find hidden serious diseases beyond the purpose of the exam, is emerging as a key topic in the medical AI industry.

A clinical study that used Coreline Soft's chest CT lung nodule analysis solution ‘AVIEW LCS’ to detect early lung cancer lesions that are easily overlooked in neck CT readings was published in the latest issue of the international journal ‘Korean Journal of Radiology.’ Neck CT includes part of the lung apex at the bottom of the scan range, but because readers focus on the neck area, small lung lesions at the edges were often missed.

Researchers at a Korean tertiary hospital retrospectively followed 81,794 adults who had neck CT scans in 2008~2024 and found 123 cases among patients later diagnosed with lung cancer in which the lesion had already appeared on an earlier neck CT. In 80 of them, or 65.0%, the reading report noted no lung lesion at all. The missed group took a median of 27.5 months to final diagnosis, and the share with worsening in any of T·N·M was 47.5%, more than 4 times that of the group detected immediately (11.6%).

When the team applied AVIEW LCS to the 80 missed cases, it flagged 41 of the 80 (sensitivity 51.3%) even though the chest-only algorithm was not retrained for neck CT. Further validation, such as false-positive rate and specificity, remains, but the study is seen as providing exploratory evidence that AI built for a specific body region can serve as a complementary safety net on images of other regions.

Coreline Soft is pursuing a ‘One CT, Multi-Disease’ strategy that analyzes lung nodules, COPD and emphysema, and coronary artery calcification at once from a single chest CT. Its revenue in the first half of 2026 rose 45.7% year on year, and overseas revenue rose 123.0%.

Large language models (LLMs) rarely recommend unnecessary care in Choosing Wisely tests, though thyroid ultrasound is more susceptible, suggest findings published October 19 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

A team led by Dean Ariel, MD, from Clalit Health Services in Tel Aviv used 15 Choosing Wisely recommendations to develop 225 scenarios, then tested six commercial LLMs that generated 4,050 responses using a prompt from the clinician perspective.

LLM-recommended overuse occurred in 5.4% of cases, and none in eight of 15 recommendations. Two accounted for most of it: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental sub-centimeter nodule (42.8% of responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (28.3%). False restraint occurred in 0.6% of cases, highest for PSA screening at 3.3%.

Thyroid ultrasound for small incidental nodules is the only recommendation in the study with active disagreement between society guidelines. “What divides them, and what the models confronted, is precisely whether to image,” the authors wrote.
An accompanying editorial called for studies using real-life cases, describing the work as the first published study to explicitly address overuse.

Artificial intelligence-powered quantitative CT analysis is capable of identifying signs of pulmonary fibrosis months before clinical diagnosis, according to a new multicenter study published in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society.

The retrospective study evaluated 509 patients with fibrotic interstitial lung disease at the University of Chicago, Weill Cornell Medicine and the University of Alabama at Birmingham, using Brainomix's e-Lung, an FDA-cleared quantitative CT tool. Boehringer Ingelheim funded the study.

These measures identified radiological progression an average of 16 months before clinical pulmonary fibrosis diagnosis, reaching up to 28 months at one center. They also detected progression in a substantial proportion of patients considered clinically stable at the time of their exam.

A higher baseline weighted reticulovascular score was associated with increased risk of future pulmonary fibrosis, while a 1.5% change in total disease extent on serial CT was associated with increased mortality. Brainomix and Boehringer Ingelheim plan to continue through PROGRESS-PPF, a prospective, multicenter U.S. study.

blocks.cap: Healthcare organizations will be able to find developer-created Connectors on Epic Showroom starting in March 2027. (ismagilov/GettyImages)

blocks.x: Epic launched "Connectors," which let developers connect their apps to Epic's AI tools: patient-facing assistant Emmie, clinician assistant Art and Penny, its revenue cycle and operations AI, plus custom agents health systems build in Agent Factory. It was announced ahead of the Open@Epic conference.

In Epic's examples, a Connector pulls an arrival time from an ambulance app so the ED can prepare, and Emmie places a hospitalized patient's meal order directly in the dietary app. Agents can chain several Connectors into one multi-step workflow.

Epic will initially use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the standard. Health systems review what each Connector can read and change before enabling it, and Epic will charge developers to list in Showroom (pricing undisclosed).
"There will not be new autonomous actions taken as a result of these capabilities," said Epic VP Johnston Thayer. Testing with some health system partners begins by the end of the year.

Microsoft AI says its diagnostic system, MAI-DxO, is 1.7 times more accurate than physicians on common US emergency-department presentations from MIMIC-IV-ED, and more than twice as accurate on complex NEJM cases. The work is published in Science.

The paper introduces the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark (SDBench): 304 complex NEJM cases plus typical MIMIC-IV-ED cases, where AI or physicians start with limited information and choose what to request next. MAI-DxO operates like a panel of virtual physicians, debating over several rounds and weighing each test’s value against its cost.

According to Microsoft, MAI-DxO achieved 83% accuracy on NEJM cases versus 22% for physicians without reference resources and 36% with them, and 80% versus 47% on emergency-department cases. One cost-optimised configuration reached 81% at less than half the cost of comparative systems.

Microsoft is open-sourcing SDBench for select NEJM cases and will run a prospective study with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, measuring performance against physicians’ independent assessments.

The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) will prepare approval and review guidelines for medicines developed using artificial intelligence (AI) by December this year. The aim is to ease the uncertainty drugmakers have faced: AI is increasingly used to discover drug candidates and predict toxicity, but there has been no separate standard for evaluating this work during approval review.

blocks.cap: Photo: The Medical Newspaper DB.

blocks.x: The plan for rationalizing regulation in the bio sector was unveiled at the 2nd plenary meeting of the Regulatory Rationalization Committee, chaired by the President, on the 23rd.

Until now, even when drugmakers used AI to discover drug candidates or predict toxicity, it was hard to judge what data to prepare for approval review. The U.S. FDA and Europe's EMA released joint guidelines this year setting out 10 basic principles the industry should follow in AI-based drug development, and the MFDS plans to reflect such international regulatory trends.

The government expects that using AI could cut traditional drug development costs, which average 1 trillion to 2 trillion won (1조~2조원), by up to 50%. Director General Shin Jun-su said, “As the number of medicines developed using AI technology grows, we will develop clear and specific review guidelines.”

The ministry will also pursue exempting water-soluble injectables with identical ingredients and excipients from submitting equivalence data, simplifying submission requirements for over-the-counter drugs with minor formulation differences, and a one-stop integrated review for digital combination medicines that incorporate AI and software.

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports clinical decisions, but human oversight is protective only if clinicians recognize and resist erroneous output. The authors systematically reviewed controlled and real-world studies of clinician responses to incorrect automated advice. Forty-six reports represented 41 independent cohort clusters, including 40 core cohorts.

Across three adjusted cohorts, clinician correctness was substantially higher with correct than incorrect automated advice (pooled OR 10.19, 95% CI 7.43–13.98). In four real-world computerized ECG studies, 26.6% of erroneous interpretations were not corrected or recognized (95% CI 6.4–65.6%).

Contemporary AI and large language model studies also documented harmful reliance but were too heterogeneous for pooling. Patient-level adverse events were reported in one retrospective cohort. Human oversight should be evaluated as an error-interception capability rather than assumed to ensure safety, the authors conclude.

The Korean Pharmaceutical Association (President Kwon Young-hee) is moving ahead in earnest with developing a ‘pharmacist work-support AI’ to assist pharmacists’ professional judgment and patient counseling. It is a pharmacy AI transformation (AX) project that applies AI to checking drug information, drug reviews, counseling preparation and record-keeping, and the association plans to build a common work-support base that member pharmacists nationwide can use at no cost.

The association selected AI company Selvik (셀빅) as its development partner and began building the system in July. The polypharmacy counseling support service under development analyzes a patient’s medications and counseling information, presents the drug problems and counseling questions a pharmacist should check first along with their evidence and sources, and supports voice summaries and counseling records. Final review, professional judgment and patient counseling are carried out by the pharmacist directly.

The field test is recruiting around 30 consultant pharmacists (30명 내외) with experience in the polypharmacy management program. Applications run from the 21st to the 25th, and testing runs from the 26th to the end of November. Participating pharmacists will receive a small reward.
Lee Yoon-pyo, director of information and communications, said, “AI should not be a technology that replaces pharmacists but a means that helps pharmacists make fuller use of their expertise.”

National healthcare groups representing hospitals, health systems, physicians and telehealth companies told the FDA they don't want to be held responsible for the safety and performance of medical devices that use generative AI, arguing that developers should shoulder that burden.

The American Hospital Association, American Medical Association and American Telemedicine Association said monitoring such devices — including chatbots and tools that synthesize medical information — would place too heavy a load on providers, particularly small and rural practices. They also asked the FDA to create ways for providers to report problems.

“Manufacturers should remain responsible for the safety and performance of the devices they sell,” said ATA Action, the telemedicine group's lobbying arm. Hospitals added that a lack of transparency into how the models work makes flaws hard for providers to spot.

The comments responded to the FDA's request for feedback on its proposed approach to regulating generative AI-enabled devices, which accept open-ended inputs and can produce different outputs to similar inputs. Provider groups largely backed its plan to assess risk by the actions a device performs, though the AHA said action alone may not predict risk, and the AMA noted a human in the loop does not necessarily mitigate it.

WEDI suggested an adverse-event reporting process and “nutrition” labels for AI tools. The FDA's Rick Abramson said the agency plans to post draft guidance on generative AI-enabled devices in the coming months.

[Medical News·Daily Bosa = Reporter Oh In-gyu] Clinician fatigue in healthcare has reached its peak, driven by chronic staffing shortages and heavy paperwork. To address this, efforts are growing to bring next-generation AI technologies such as large language models (LLM) into clinical settings and improve day-to-day working conditions.

In line with this trend, medical artificial intelligence (AI) company AITRICS (CEO Kim Kwang-joon) is teaming up with Kangbuk Samsung Hospital to ease the long-standing burden of documentation in clinical practice. The move follows its recent selection as a consortium participant in the '2026 AI Transformation (AX) Support Program' run by Seoul AI Hub.

Through the project, AITRICS will begin developing an LLM-based AX platform that automates clinical medical records and transforms in-hospital workflows. The strategy is to maximize care efficiency by replacing the information checks and record-keeping repeated every day on the front lines with AI.

As partner, Kangbuk Samsung Hospital will play a central role, closely analyzing real outpatient and nursing environments to define the specific tasks AI will be applied to. It will also specify essential functions and validation criteria tailored to the doctors and nurses who do the hands-on work.

The development work comes down to three main tasks: ▲advancing the accumulated medication and diagnosis histories of patients in outpatient care ▲summarizing key progress from large volumes of imaging reports such as CT·MRI ▲converting voice conversations during nursing handoffs to text (STT) and summarizing their content. The core aim is for AI to condense vast amounts of medical data quickly and accurately and deliver it at the right time.

Kangbuk Samsung Hospital staff will take part directly from the early planning and development stages to evaluate usability and closely examine clinical validity. The two institutions plan to use this collaboration as a springboard to secure technical versatility, so the finished platform can later be readily adopted by other medical institutions.
AITRICS CEO Kim Kwang-joon repeatedly stressed the practical effectiveness of AI technology grounded firmly in on-site needs.

"The main goal of this project is to complete a customized AX platform that puts the voices of the field first and can be immediately integrated into real hospital systems," Kim said. "We will do our best to make advanced LLM technology a catalyst for digital innovation in healthcare that not only meaningfully reduces clinicians' workload but also changes the paradigm of overall hospital operations."
Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh have designed an AI model they believe will help make breast cancer imaging AI more trustworthy.

Its deep neural network is trained to estimate uncertainty alongside its diagnostic predictions. The method, called uncertainty-weighted learning, generates a prediction and an uncertainty score, flagging cases where the output may be less dependable and an AI result may need a radiologist's second look.

Shandong Wu, PhD, a professor of radiology at Pitt, led the work with doctoral student Jiren Li and Dooman Arefan, PhD, using the Bridges-2 supercomputer at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center to train and evaluate the models.
The team hopes to extend the approach beyond mammography, but the work is still early and needs further validation across patient populations and imaging settings.
Seizure semiology offers clues for localizing the epileptogenic zone (EZ) in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, but its interpretation varies across clinicians and institutions.

EpiSemoLLM was developed from 1,372 surgically verified semiology–EZ pairs drawn from 392 published studies and a cohort from Far Eastern Memorial Hospital, combining parameter-efficient fine-tuning with structured epilepsy knowledge and literature-based evidence retrieval.

It achieved the strongest overall localization among the language models evaluated and performed better than the median epileptologist in the held-out cohort, with similar findings in an external cohort of 83 cases from Taipei Veterans General Hospital.
Clinicians performed better in frontal and insular localization. Prospective validation is needed before routine clinical use.

The FDA has cleared Elucid's FFR-IQ software for noninvasive estimation of fractional flow reserve from coronary CT angiography (FFR-CT). The AI-based technology incorporates coronary anatomy and plaque composition into its estimate of coronary physiology.

Elucid said physicians wanted a more accurate FFR-CT algorithm that considered other factors affecting hemodynamics. It is now the third vendor to offer FFR-CT commercially in the U.S., after Heartflow in 2016 and KeyaMed in 2022.

Clearance was based on ELUCIDATE FFR-CT study data showing an overall sensitivity of 92.2% and specificity of 93.1%. The algorithm draws on plaque measurements from Elucid's Plaque-IQ software, cleared in October 2024.
Results of the ELUCIDATE FFR-CT study will be presented Nov. 1 at TCT 2026 in San Diego.

Five AI tools that can help identify prostate cancer “more accurately” on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans will be made available to doctors, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has announced.

NICE has recommended that the technologies be used in the NHS to help detect prostate cancer on MRI while further evidence on their use and accuracy is generated. The tools “are designed to help radiologists by highlighting areas on a prostate MRI scan where cancer might be present,” it said.

NICE concluded that the technologies “have the potential” to improve the accuracy and consistency of prostate MRI interpretation, particularly in settings without specialist expertise. But it added that further evidence was needed to understand how the tools would perform in routine NHS practice.

Researchers with NYU Langone Health may have identified a new way to predict heart transplant rejection without the need for an invasive biopsy. Their findings were published in the Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation.

The researchers trained AI models on more than 5,300 ECG readings from 389 adult heart transplant recipients between 2018 and 2024. One model used ECG data alone; a second combined ECG data with the results of two blood tests, AlloMap and AlloSure, traditionally used to predict rejection risk but with a high false-positive rate.

In a test group of 38 heart transplant recipients, the combined model performed better. Two patients experienced rejection. The AI model correctly identified 97% of patients who were not experiencing rejection, while the blood-test-only approach incorrectly indicated that 19 patients needed a biopsy.

“Heart transplantation is a major, resource-intensive procedure, and rejection is common but treatable if caught in time,” senior author Lior Jankelson, MD, PhD, said. As a next step, the researchers plan to test the AI model in more patients at several transplant centers.

Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models can anticipate when older heart failure patients may start to experience functional decline, according to new findings published in the Journal of Cardiac Failure.

Researchers explored data from more than 6,000 patients 65 years old or older who were hospitalized for heart failure and prescribed rehabilitation; the median age was 82. The machine learning model estimates a patient’s one-year risk of functional maintenance, functional decline (a transition to a housebound/bedridden lifestyle) or death.

Overall, 32.5% of patients experienced functional decline and more than 14% died within one year of discharge. The model, which used 77 different factors, identified these outcomes with improved accuracy compared to the Kihon Checklist screening tool.

“Instead of asking only whether a patient will survive, we need to ask whether they will be able to maintain the life they value after discharge,” lead author Kanji Yamada, PT, PhD, of Juntendo University in Japan, said.

blocks.cap: As Doximity ramps up its investment in clinical AI tools, the partnership with Wolters Kluwer positions Ask as the front door to clinical knowledge.

blocks.x: Doximity inked a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to embed UpToDate's evidence-based clinical content directly within Doximity Ask, the company’s AI clinical decision support tool.

In the coming weeks, at health systems that use both products, clinicians will see an answer based on UpToDate’s 13,000 clinical topics and best practice guides alongside Doximity Ask’s response, without leaving the Ask workflow.

The company aims to become a leading AI platform for doctors, scaling a clinical AI suite that includes its ambient note-taking tool Scribe and Ask. A year ago, Doximity acquired clinical AI company Pathway.

“Every frontier model has read all the same journals. UpToDate stands alone as a gold standard reference from experienced physicians about what happens when there isn't an RCT,” Doximity CEO Jeff Tangney told Fierce Healthcare.
Doximity’s membership includes more than 85% of all U.S. doctors, and its clinical AI tools, including Ask, have been deployed across more than 165 health systems, according to the company.
Competition in clinical AI is intensifying. Wolters Kluwer has also partnered with Epic and Abridge to integrate UpToDate into their AI-powered CDS tools.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Overview of the AI-SP architecture and three-phase evaluation.

blocks.x: Standardized patients (SPs) are central to clinical communication training but remain constrained by cost, scalability, and reliance on trained actors. The authors present AI standardized patients (AI-SPs), large language model–driven simulators built on a three-layer information architecture that adaptively modulates disclosure according to learner skill.

In Phase 1, blinded expert assessment of 350 simulated consultations generated by five frontier LLMs showed learner skill level accounted for more performance variation than model choice (η2 = 0.31 vs. 0.06). In Phase 1b, 155 live student consultations revealed systematic failures to elicit safety-critical information.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: The three-layer AI-SP system prompt design.

blocks.x: In a Phase 2 three-arm pilot randomized study (n = 58), OSCE performance gains with AI-SP training did not differ significantly from human SP training; the trial was designed to estimate effect sizes, not to demonstrate equivalence. Self-efficacy gains were numerically largest with AI-SPs, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Eko Health has received FDA clearance for Core 300, a new AI-enabled stethoscope that offers both traditional analog and advanced digital listening capabilities.

Clinicians can instantly switch from traditional to digital listening when evaluating pediatric and adult patients. Digital listening includes up to 35x amplification, noise cancellation and real-time heart data displayed on the device.
The stethoscopes can also connect to the Eko App or Eko's FDA-cleared AI models, and the battery was designed to last for weeks at a time.

“Eko has delivered more than 750,000 devices, and Core 300 is the next step toward bringing early disease detection confidence to every healthcare professional,” said Connor Landgraf, co-founder and CEO of Eko Health.
The device is now available to U.S. consumers, and a gradual international launch is underway.

The use of an AI-driven ambient scribe in outpatient practice was associated with reductions in time spent taking notes and increased note length, but other productivity measures were largely unchanged, researchers found.

Among all users, median note-active time decreased from 21 minutes to 18.6 minutes and median note length increased from 4,854 to 5,187 characters after clinicians enrolled in Heidi, according to Jennifer P. Stevens, MD, of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, and colleagues. However, no differences were seen in same-day or after-hours note closure, or in clinical productivity, they reported in Annals of Internal Medicine.

Of 902 clinicians at the 14-hospital Beth Israel Lahey Health system who met inclusion criteria, 67.0% used Heidi at least once. Among high users, the immediate reduction in note-active time was significantly larger (-2.50 minutes) than among enrolled nonusers (-0.29 minutes) and low users (-0.78 minutes).

In an accompanying editorial, Kirsten Ostherr, PhD, MPH, of Rice University noted the study didn't capture time spent editing notes within Heidi, which "raises an important question about whether ambient scribes relocate documentation burden rather than reduce it."

The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved House Bill 1925, which includes disclosure rules for healthcare facilities and restrictions on insurers' reliance on AI during utilization review, by a 144-59 vote on Sept. 30. The amended bill was referred to the Senate Institutional Sustainability and Innovation Committee on Oct. 14 and remains pending in the Senate.

If enacted, the legislation would require healthcare facilities, including imaging centers, to disclose their use of AI in clinical decision-making through website postings and written patient notifications, once per episode of care. Facilities would be required to review AI system performance at least annually and ensure that the technology does not supersede providers' independent clinical judgment.

Before issuing or upholding an adverse coverage determination, such as a prior authorization denial, individuals conducting utilization review would be required to review clinical records and make their own independent judgment rather than relying on AI recommendations without human oversight. The American College of Radiology expects similar proposals during 2027 state legislative sessions.

Seoul, South Korea-based AI developer Coreline Soft has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for Aview Aorta Metrics, its software for quantitative aortic assessment on chest CT.

The software automatically segments the aorta from chest CT images, classifies aortic zones, and measures the diameter of each zone, according to the vendor. It also provides straightened curved planar reformation, cross-sectional, and 3D views, as well as analysis reports, Coreline Soft said.

The clearance is Coreline Soft's 13th FDA 510(k) clearance, according to the company. Aview Aorta Metrics joins the firm's Aview platform for analysis of multiple diseases on chest CT, which includes Aview LCS and Aview Lung Nodule CAD for lung nodule detection and analysis, and Aview CAC for coronary artery calcium scoring on noncontrast chest CT.

Chest x-ray reading accuracy declines significantly in fatigued radiology residents after overnight shifts, and AI offers little help, according to a study from Aachen University Hospital in Germany published October 22 in European Radiology.

Ten radiology residents each interpreted three sets of 33 bedside chest x-rays, two sessions before a first-call on-site night shift and one immediately after, the latter with and without AI assistance from a model the team had previously developed.

blocks.cap: Technical setup and customized DICOM viewer with screen-based eye tracking; with AI assistance, the template was pre-filled with the model's suggestions. European Radiology

blocks.x: Six of 10 residents were classified as fatigued. Their diagnostic accuracy declined significantly post-shift, from a κ of 0.71 to 0.61 (p < 0.001); non-fatigued readers showed a smaller but still significant decline (κ, 0.72 to 0.65). AI assistance did not significantly improve accuracy in either group, and shortened reporting times only in non-fatigued readers (by 9.9 seconds).

"Night-shift-induced fatigue impaired diagnostic accuracy without slowing reporting speed, raising patient safety concerns. The utilized AI model did not restore pre-shift performance," the researchers noted.
Rivanna has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for BoneEnhance, a machine-learning software module for its Accuro XV diagnostic ultrasound system.

BoneEnhance identifies bone and surrounding tissues within volumetric datasets acquired by the system’s 3D probe and highlights them with color-coded overlays on 2D B-mode images, while leaving the original anatomical data visible, according to the company. In an independent test set of 233 volumetric datasets from five sites, per-volume label prediction accuracy ranged from 95.1% to 100%, Rivanna said.

Rivanna is also developing an investigational module to help clinicians evaluate potential extremity fractures on ultrasound images. The firm said the work has been supported by the U.S. Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority.

ChatGPT-5 missed approximately half of distal radius fractures on plain x-rays when provided a single binary fracture-or-not prompt, according to a study published October 26 in Emergency Radiology by a group from the Rambam Health Care Campus in Haifa, Israel.

The researchers submitted 370 anteroposterior distal radius x-rays from the Stanford MURA dataset to ChatGPT-5 via its public web interface in a zero-shot approach. They asked, “Is there a fracture in this X-ray? Answer with yes or no.”

blocks.cap: Representative ChatGPT-5 outputs against the reference standard. Emergency Radiology

blocks.x: Fracture prevalence in the analyzed sample was 45.9% (170/370). ChatGPT-5 missed 83 fractures, demonstrating a sensitivity of 51.2% and a specificity of 70.5%, with overall accuracy of 61.6%. False negatives significantly exceeded false positives.
"Put plainly: a general-purpose chatbot should not be used to decide whether a radiograph shows a fracture," the researchers wrote.

PHILADELPHIA -- An AI-based triage approach could lower turnaround times in emergency settings, suggest findings presented October 27 at the SIIM-CAIMI 2026 meeting by Ai Tong, PhD, from the University of Washington in Seattle.

blocks.cap: Ai Tong, PhD, reports on her team's use of an AI-based ICH triaging approach.

blocks.x: The AI triage system achieved 79.3% sensitivity, 94.2% specificity, and an F1 score of 0.78 against NLP-derived ICH labels. Among ICH-positive exams, AI triaging reduced report turnaround time from a median of 214 minutes to 201 minutes (p = 0.03).
Among 10,898 pre-AI and 9,317 post-AI emergency encounters, AI-positive cases led to shorter time to admission (median 423.5 minutes) than AI-negative cases (523.0 minutes; p = 0.004).
“This [study] is early and only correlational,” Tong said, adding the findings suggest AI triaging’s clinical impact extends beyond radiology efficiency.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical medical imaging has advanced diagnostics but also poses challenges in maintaining long-term reliability as input data change. To address this, we present MMC+, a modular framework for scalable drift monitoring that builds on our CheXstray framework for real-time drift detection using multi-modal data concordance (MMC).

MMC+ provides a flexible architecture that enables cost-effective continuous performance monitoring in real-world healthcare settings. The framework’s capabilities include aggregating information from multiple data streams using statistical tests or distance metrics, leveraging foundation model embeddings to remove the need for site-specific encoder training, and quantifying uncertainty to better communicate drift significance.

Validated with data from Massachusetts General Hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, MMC+ effectively detects significant data shifts that correlate with performance changes and indicates when AI systems may deviate from acceptable performance bounds. The code for MMC+ is publicly available, promoting broader adoption of AI solutions in clinical settings.

blocks.cap: Accuracy is critical to helping members build trust with the tool and use it most effectively, said Craig Kurtzweil, chief data and analytics officer at UnitedHealthcare. (UnitedHealthcare)

blocks.x: Earlier this year, UnitedHealthcare unveiled Avery, a generative AI companion aimed at supporting care coordination for its members. At the time, the tool was available to about 6.5 million of its members in employer plans and 160,000 people enrolled in Medicare Advantage. Now, the insurer is expanding access to 21 million of its members.
To date, the company has found that Avery has resolved 90% of its member interactions, and in the remaining 10% of cases, can complete a handoff to a human advocate to offer member support.

Kurtzweil said a key piece of what makes Avery work is that it's built on "ground truth systems" that create a critical data foundation for the platform. Avery can provide key details on deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, provider networks, pricing and claims processing.

The team is also building out additional functionality for Avery, including an option for it to call providers and schedule appointments on the member's behalf. UnitedHealthcare intends to ultimately ensure that all of its enrollees can tap into the tool.

blocks.cap: Caristo's fat attenuation index (FAI) AI-assessment for coronary inflammation in CCTA scans can visualize patient's residual cardiac risk not seen on traditional cardiac assessments.

blocks.x: The first U.S. study of Caristo Diagnostics’ FDA-cleared CaRi-Heart technology for coronary inflammation detection found a large number of asymptomatic adult patients were actually at an elevated risk of cardiac events.

The study, conducted by the Biograph concierge medicine clinic, used Caristo's fat attenuation index (FAI) AI algorithm on preventive cardiac CT scans and found inflammation in 42.9% of study participants. Of these, 17.9% had very high inflammation levels in at least one major artery. Approximately 47% of participants who had no detectable coronary plaque were found to have elevated coronary perivascular inflammation, which raises their risk of a cardiac event.

“Crucially, no routine blood biomarker, lipid metric, or clinical risk score could identify these individuals with inflamed coronary arteries,” said Michael Doney, MD, executive medical director at Biograph. He added that more research is needed to validate this and establish the prognostic value of FAI.
The FDA granted de novo market clearance for the CaRi-Heart technology in late July. It is the first technology that can visualize and clearly quantify coronary inflammation using FAI scores.

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for fracture detection perform strongly in controlled settings, but prospective real-world evidence is limited. In a three-month deployment in one emergency department, thirteen radiographers in a radiographer-led screening programme independently interpreted 2496 consecutive musculoskeletal examinations (one radiographer per examination), reviewed output from a commercial deep-learning system, then recorded a final decision, giving 2496 paired reads against a radiologist reference standard.

Standalone AI sensitivity was 75.6%, falling to 46.2% for subtle fractures, below the radiographers’ baseline sensitivity of 91.6%. Radiographers’ baseline accuracy was high (97.6%; specificity 99.0%) and improved modestly with AI assistance (98.0%; exact McNemar p = 0.0064). With AI assistance, radiographers corrected 11 errors and introduced 1, a net gain of 10 cases.

Radiographers changed their decision in only 11 of 729 discordant cases, and most negative interactions were correct AI recommendations not adopted. No or incomplete AI output was returned for 8.8% of acquired examinations.

AI assistance delivered a small, selective benefit arising from complementary rather than superior algorithmic performance. Operational reliability proved as consequential as diagnostic accuracy. Downstream clinical outcomes were not measured.
Stanford Health developed an in-house large language model pipeline to flag critical results in pediatric radiology reports, presented by Pooja Pathak at SIIM-CAIMI 2026 in Philadelphia.

The pipeline covers six categories: increased intracranial pressure, non-accidental trauma, malpositioned feeding tubes, unsuspected pneumoperitoneum, portal venous gas and tension pneumothorax. It runs locally on Llama 3.3 (70B), so no data leaves the institution and no commercial tool is needed.

In validation on 916 reports, it reached 99.7% sensitivity and 97.9% specificity. From August 2024 to July 2026, it flagged 1,297 critical results among 182,047 finalized reports, with feeding tube malpositions the most common.
Turnaround times and communication documentation stayed stable during deployment. Future work will focus on making the pipeline more context-aware and testing newer models.

Daewoong Pharmaceutical has built an AI-based real-time bed monitoring system at Ajou University Hospital. The company said on the 26th that it supplied its smart bed monitoring system thynC and began operating it in 342 beds across 7 wards.

Ajou University Hospital started with its thoracic surgery and cardiology wards and has extended thynC to its emergency ward and its integrated nursing care service wards. Based on current results, it plans to consider expanding the rollout to up to 1100 beds.

The rollout focuses on quickly catching changes in the condition of patients with severe illness and of patients who need close observation before and after surgery. The aim is to support patient care by medical staff through continuous monitoring of vital signs, even in general wards.

thynC uses a wearable biosensor worn by the patient to measure electrocardiogram, heart rate, pulse rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation in real time. It offers AI-based detection and classification of falls and emergency arrhythmias, and when it detects an abnormal sign it shows an alarm on the ward monitoring screen to help medical staff respond.

Key vital data are linked to the electronic medical record (EMR), which automatically records the latest readings at 60-second intervals. This reduces the burden of repetitive manual entry on medical staff and lets them view and save, in report form, the vital signs and ECG events measured during the hospital stay.

Ajou University Hospital began installing equipment and building infrastructure last year and optimized the system for clinical settings through August this year. From September it expanded operations centered on thoracic surgery and cardiology, and this month it extended coverage to the emergency ward and the integrated nursing care service wards.

It also built a wireless monitoring system using wearable devices and fixed gateways inside the wards. Because vital signs can be checked while patients move around the ward, the system is used to observe cardiovascular patients before and after surgery and to manage emergency ward patients.

Han Sang-wook, president of Ajou University Medical Center, said, “We expect to further strengthen patient safety because we can check inpatients’ key vital signs in real time and detect abnormal signs early.” He added, “Based on the results of the 342 beds now in operation, we are also considering expanding the rollout to all 1100 beds, and we will continue to actively use digital technology to build a safer and smarter care environment.”

Daewoong Pharmaceutical is expanding thynC-based smart wards, centered on tertiary general hospitals and major regional hospitals. According to the company, as of October this year it had been installed at 218 medical institutions nationwide, for a cumulative 2만54 beds. It plans to support on-site operations with usage guides that reflect each institution’s patient characteristics and operating environment.

Lee Chang-jae, CEO of Daewoong Pharmaceutical, said, “It is meaningful to take part in building smart wards that strengthen patient safety by supplying thynC to Ajou University Hospital, which plays a core role in severe and emergency care in southern Gyeonggi.” He added, “We will continue to strengthen our cooperation with Ajou University Hospital and support the digital transformation of medical institutions in southern Gyeonggi and the creation of patient-centered care environments.”

blocks.cap: The UT Dell Medical Center, slated to open in 2030, will integrate artificial intelligence and advanced tech directly into patient care and clinical training. (UT Dell Medicine)

blocks.x: The University of Texas at Austin unveiled Tuesday a unified academic health system, called UT Dell Medicine, that brings its clinics, Dell Medical School and the upcoming UT Dell Medical Center under one banner.

Site clearing begins this month to build a new AI-native medical center in North Austin, slated to open in 2030 with an estimated price tag of about $5 billion, anchored by a $750 million gift from the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation. It will feature a 300-to-500-bed specialty hospital, an outpatient clinic and a full emergency department.

UT leaders aim to build AI and other advanced technologies into the hospital's infrastructure from the ground up. The medical center expects to have 20,000 to 30,000 sensors throughout the facility, and is designing for extensive use of robotics, including automated transportation of medications, supplies, linens and food.

The vision is for the hospital to “become an intelligent member of the care team,” said Claudia Lucchinetti, M.D. UT Dell Medicine also plans to use AI, predictive tools and data to shift care toward earlier detection and prevention.

BALTIMORE -- An artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool could be a last resort for couples wanting to conceive a biological child who had been told they have no sperm, researchers said at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) annual meeting.

The Sperm Tracking and Recovery (STAR) system, developed by Hemant Suryawanshi, PhD, of Columbia University Fertility Center and colleagues, uses high-speed imaging, real-time AI, and microfluidic technology to take two million images, assess them, and isolate the sperm detected by AI into a small volume.
In 10 spiked samples, STAR found sperm in all 10 cases while the manual expert only found it three times. STAR found 167 sperm while the human only found four -- a 41-fold difference.
Among 175 consecutive men deemed sperm-negative by manual examination, STAR detected at least one sperm in 26% of the samples, and in 29% of those who had undergone TESE.

Sperm identified with STAR has led to at least three live births in which the recovered sperm were used for ICSI or cryopreservation. A major limitation is user-friendliness: STAR requires a highly-trained technician to run it.

Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. The authors developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Multi-dimensional validation framework for an agentic LLM-based irAE detection system.

blocks.x: Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F1 was 0.72–0.79.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: Multi-stage agentic architecture for irAE detection, grading, attribution and certainty assessment.

blocks.x: In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min (P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff's α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

OpenEvidence is expanding its footprint in New York City through a partnership with NYU Langone Health. Its AI-powered clinical evidence platform is embedded directly into NYU Langone's Epic EHR workflows, spanning its hospitals, ambulatory network and the Family Health Centers, and reaching physicians training at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and the NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine. NYU Langone has more than 12 million outpatient visits annually and over 6,000 physicians and faculty.

Clinicians will be able to ask complex clinical questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in peer-reviewed medical literature and read against the patient's own clinical record, all without leaving their Epic workflow. "Putting OpenEvidence inside the chart at NYU Langone means the world's medical literature is now in the room for every one of the twelve million visits this system supports each year," said founder and CEO Daniel Nadler.

The company says roughly two-thirds of U.S. physicians use its platform; 1.2 million verified U.S. clinicians consulted it 45 million times in October. It already has deployments at NewYork-Presbyterian and Mount Sinai and an oncology partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering. A JAMA study found nearly 1 million U.S. clinicians submitted 271 million queries from January 2024 to June 2026, 51.9% related to clinical decision-making.

Research released by Doximity shows that its dose verification tool outperformed general-use AI models, which it says are rife with errors. Doximity says it tested a handful of large language models released in 2026 with more than 8,500 clinical dosing questions covering more than 2,200 FDA-approved drugs.

Freshly approved drugs had five times the odds of an error. Of the errors detected, 13.2% were minor, 43% were significant and 3.4% were potentially lethal. The most common mistake was failing to adjust doses for age, kidney function or drug interactions, even when that information was given in the question.

Doximity claimed its new verification tool, DoseCheck, was correct 99.9% of the time; it frames the tool as a safety net within Doximity Ask. "The failure modes we saw aren't unique to dosing," said Dr. Louis-Antoine Mullie, chief AI researcher at Doximity.

The research comes as Anthropic and OpenAI enter healthcare. Studies have landed on both sides: Stanford and Harvard researchers found clinically specialized tools outperformed general-purpose models, while another team this summer found the opposite.

blocks.cap: X-ray image of human knee joint showing femur, tibia, fibula, and patella in anteroposterior view

blocks.x: HOPPR is launching a beta version of its FS MSK Whole-Body Narrative Model, a vision-language foundation model that generates draft findings text for musculoskeletal (MSK) radiographs using up to three views per study.

The model was trained on about 674,000 outpatient MSK studies covering the spine, thorax and chest wall, upper extremity, and pelvis and lower extremity, according to the vendor. It focuses on describing abnormalities rather than normal anatomy. HOPPR said it evaluated the model against 26 MSK finding categories, including fracture, degenerative joint and spine changes, alignment, and hardware.

The model is designed as a software component for developers building radiology reporting and workflow applications, and HOPPR’s Forward Deployed Services team will customize and integrate it for each organization’s data and workflows, the company said. It is not cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and is not intended for diagnostic use, the firm said.
Online scheduling company Zocdoc is now letting AI agents search for providers and book appointments on behalf of patients.

Agents must register with Zocdoc to gain access and obtain patient consent before booking or canceling an appointment on its online platform, the company said Wednesday. Google Gemini, Amazon Health AI, and text- and call-based AI agent Instinct are already connected, and other agents can apply for access with or without a human’s help.
“I would say that welcoming agents the way we are is a bit of a contrarian move,” said Dr. Oliver Kharraz, founder and CEO of Zocdoc.

blocks.cap: Zocdoc says AI agent traffic on its platform has grown nearly 30-fold since July — now the company is opening its booking platform to them directly.

blocks.x: An approved agent can plug into Zocdoc’s AI backend to sift through its provider directory, check a clinician’s availability, verify insurance and book an appointment, checking in with the patient before making any final decisions.

In return, Zocdoc expects agents to obtain patient consent and protect patient and provider data; they are not allowed to train themselves based on the data, resell it or republish it. Zocdoc did not specify how it plans to ensure that agents respect that agreement.
“Our mission is to give power to the patient. If they want to delegate the booking to an AI agent, then we should give them the frictionless access to care that they want,” Kharraz said.

Building on its recent guidance for clinical AI governance, the American Medical Association on Thursday gave a deeper breakdown of how different parties should be responsible for decisions, actions and failures involving the technology. The framework from AMA's Center for Digital Health and AI addresses liability issues it said existing frameworks leave unanswered, which could leave physicians facing "liability for risks they cannot reasonably prevent, while patients may struggle to seek remedies when AI causes harm."

The framework "recognizes that multiple parties may bear liability for the use of AI when something goes wrong," aligning accountability with a party's ability to prevent harm. Physicians should "be responsible for the clinical judgment they can meaningfully exercise, based on the system's intended use, known limitations and the information available at the point of care," and may decline an unproven AI system without penalty.

"As AI assumes more clinical functions, developers, healthcare organizations and physicians each have important responsibilities," said AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D. The liability framework details one aspect of a broader clinical AI governance framework AMA unveiled earlier this month.

Missed specialist referrals in primary care pose substantial health and medico-legal risks, yet remain poorly understood. We developed an AI-supported safety system (MR-AI) to identify missed referrals from consultation notes, evaluated in a quasi-experimental study across seven primary care clinics in Singapore. MR-AI scanned ~25,000 notes weekly for referral intent without a corresponding order, achieving an estimated sevenfold increase in weekly missed referral detection (4.7 percentage point level increase; 95% CI 0.024–0.069; p < 0.001).

Of 428 cases flagged, 225 were clinician-verified, alongside 31 patient-reported cases, yielding 256 total detections. MR-AI demonstrated 99.9% specificity and 48.8% sensitivity. In a blinded one-week comparison against seven physician reviewers, MR-AI achieved a PPV of 61.8% versus a human confirmation rate of 51.8% across 83 flagged cases, while requiring approximately 41 fewer projected staff-hours.

AI-enabled surveillance substantially assisted in missed referral detection, though sustainable improvement will require complementary preventive workflow changes and future cost-effectiveness assessment.

Many adolescents seek mental health advice from general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, despite limited evaluations against youth-relevant clinical standards. Here we developed the Adolescent Mental Health AI Response Tool (AMHART), a clinician-informed instrument for auditing the presence of guideline-informed response content across seven domains, and applied it to four major AI chatbots.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Graphic summary of AMHART development and evaluation.

blocks.x: Candidate items were reviewed by clinicians for their evidence base, objectivity and clinical importance, yielding a subset with strong content validity and inter-rater reliability. We then configured a three-model large language model evaluator ensemble, assessed its agreement with human reference labels and scored multiturn conversations in which adolescent personas (varying by sex, diagnosis and symptom severity) engaged with ChatGPT-5, ChatGPT-4, Claude 4.5 and Gemini 2.5.

AMHART scores indicated greater coverage of applicable criteria for anxiety than depression and for moderate than severe presentations. The findings suggest AMHART offers a reliable, clinician-informed benchmark for evaluating chatbot responses to adolescent anxiety and depression disclosures.

Brainomix is highlighting a study showing how automated noncontrast CT analysis with the company's software may help identify patients with large hemispheric infarction. These patients are more likely to benefit from intravenous glyburide (Cirara), an investigational therapy from Remedy Pharmaceuticals, according to a post-hoc analysis of the phase III Charm trial presented at the World Stroke Conference in Seoul.

Using its Brainomix 360 Stroke software, the company measured acute infarct volume on noncontrast CT in 428 trial patients. In a subgroup of 191 patients with infarct core volumes below 125 mL, Cirara showed significantly association with improved functional outcomes on the modified Rankin Scale, including a greater likelihood of achieving a score of 0 to 3 at 90 days, the researchers found.

The findings suggest that patients could be selected for trials of the therapy without advanced imaging such as CT perfusion or MRI, Brainomix said. Cirara has not been approved by any regulatory authority.

Research Letter by Hannah T. Neprash, PhD (University of Minnesota) and Michael L. Barnett, MD, MS (Brown University). Prior authorization is "a process that requires clinicians to submit justification for specific medical services before reimbursement is offered." Historically, traditional Medicare has not required any prior authorization, with rare exceptions.

The Center for Medicare & Medicaid Innovation's Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model, a 6-year pilot that began in January 2026 in Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington, requires prior authorization for selected services and encourages participants to use artificial intelligence. There was no evidence to date on its initial impact.

Using Epic Cosmos electronic health record data, the authors compared monthly use of WISeR-targeted services in the six pilot states with all other states and Washington, D.C., over the two years before launch and the first six months after.

Relative to nonpilot states, epidural steroid injections fell about 15% and other targeted services about 20%. The drop was largest at launch: epidural steroid injections were about 21% lower in the first quarter of 2026 and about 9% lower in the second; other services went from 21% to 18%. Services slated for WISeR but never implemented showed no significant decline.
Whether the forgone care was unnecessary or needed remains unknown; the authors call for tracking persistence, appropriateness of care, patient outcomes, clinician burden and Medicare spending.

blocks.cap: Wearable device - checking progress

blocks.x: Using AI to analyze patterns from a portable cuff-based blood pressure monitor and a wrist-worn fitness tracker may help identify when adults with stage 2 high blood pressure are at increased risk of a hypertensive crisis (>180/120 mm Hg with acute end-organ damage) up to three days before it occurs, according to preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026.

The study included 4,190 adults ages 40 to 85 at one hospital in Sindh, Pakistan, followed from January 2025 to January 2026. Over the 12 months, 312 participants experienced 418 hypertensive crises. Among participants with a positive alert, about 32% experienced a crisis, while 97.4% of those without an alert remained crisis-free.

Blood pressure that did not decrease during sleep meant nearly five times the odds of an upcoming crisis; a rise of more than 35 mm Hg after waking meant nearly four times the odds. When physicians received an alert and adjusted medications within 24 hours, crises were about 61% lower and emergency department visits about 45% lower.

“If we are able to recognize an increased risk of a hypertensive crisis days before it occurs, we have an opportunity to provide earlier care,” said lead author Waleed Razzaq Chaudhry, M.D. The abstract is not peer-reviewed and findings are preliminary.

The 53 Member States of the WHO European Region have unanimously adopted the Region’s first “Roadmap for action on artificial intelligence in health”, approved during the 76th session of the WHO Regional Committee for Europe. It sets out a shared vision for integrating AI into health systems across Europe and Central Asia.

Dr Corinne Capuano, Officer-in-Charge for WHO/Europe, said: “AI is already changing health care across our region… How do we ensure AI is safe, effective and equitable? How do we protect people’s rights and earn their trust? These are challenges no country can solve alone.”

Covering 2026–2033, the roadmap has 4 priority areas: governance and leadership; ethical, regulatory and legal frameworks; data and digital infrastructure; and capacity-building, implementation support and learning. It drew on responses from 50 of the Region’s 53 Member States to the first region-wide AI readiness assessment, published in 2025.

It aligns with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the European Health Data Space and the General Data Protection Regulation, among others, and comes with an implementation guide. Member States also supported establishing a new WHO office on AI.

Researchers evaluated product name recommendations from five LLMs — GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Llama 4 and MedGemma — using 177,120 synthetic clinical vignettes spanning 123 disease–drug pairs and 1,440 sociodemographic profiles. Each vignette asked the model to recommend FDA-approved products containing a specified active ingredient.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Study design and analytical workflow.

blocks.x: The most frequently recommended product accounted for a mean of 97.5% of first-choice recommendations, and the models showed almost perfect agreement (Fleiss’ κ = 0.895). Recommendations diverged from real-world prescribing; of 51 active ingredients, 38 (74.5%) showed higher costs, an estimated annual increase of US$55.6 million.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: Consistency of LLM product recommendations across vignettes and models.

blocks.x: Models favoured originator products (OR 20.5) and those with greater online visibility (Google search counts, OR 1.70; a dedicated Wikipedia page, OR 3.00). Prompts asking for generic or lowest-cost products shifted recommendations towards generics.

A research team led by professors Jung In-hyun and Bae Sung-ah of the cardiology department at Yonsei University Yongin Severance Hospital and professor Yoon Duk-yong of the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine said on the 29th that it had recently published a study developing and validating an artificial intelligence (AI) model that predicts the likelihood of reduced heart function from chest X-ray images.

Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is usually measured by echocardiography, but because it requires equipment and skilled specialists, it has been hard to perform at smaller medical institutions. The team developed and compared two models: direct deep learning (DDL) and hybrid deep learning (HDL), which uses analysis results from the imaging AI Lunit INSIGHT CXR.

Data from 1만152 patients at Yongin Severance Hospital were used for model development, 505 patients who visited the emergency room or outpatient clinic with shortness of breath for prospective validation, and data from 3657 patients at Seoul National University Hospital for external validation.

The HDL model's AUROC was 0.85, higher than the DDL model's 0.61. In prospective validation, the HDL model scored 0.85 and the DDL model 0.57, and the HDL model's external validation AUROC was 0.73. The HDL model showed specificity of 90~97% and negative predictive value of 91~98%.

Professors Jung In-hyun and Bae Sung-ah said, "After further clinical validation, we expect it could be used as an assistive tool to screen patients suspected of reduced heart function in emergency rooms or at medical institutions with limited access to echocardiography." The results were published in the international journal Scientific Reports.

blocks.cap: Samsung Electronics has upgraded the Sleep Apnea feature on the Galaxy Watch to help users manage their sleep health more systematically. Photo=Samsung Electronics

blocks.x: Samsung Electronics said on the 28th that it has upgraded the Sleep Apnea feature on the Galaxy Watch and obtained approval from the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS). The newly approved feature uses an AI algorithm to analyze in detail the number of breathing disruptions per hour during sleep. Whereas the previous feature only detected whether signs of sleep apnea were present, the upgraded feature breaks the user's level of breathing disruption into 3 tiers: mild, occasional and frequent.

Sleep apnea is a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops or decreases during sleep, and it can lead to various complications such as high blood pressure, arrhythmia and stroke. According to the U.S. National Sleep Foundation, about 25% of men and 10% of women in the U.S. have sleep apnea, but many of them are unaware of it.

Users can access the feature through the Samsung Health Monitor app, and signs of sleep apnea can be detected by measuring at least 5 hours of sleep twice within 10 days. The feature is intended for people aged 18 or older with no prior sleep apnea diagnosis and does not replace professional medical diagnosis or consultation.

In Korea, the new feature will first be offered from November on the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, Watch9 and Galaxy Ring, then gradually extended to existing models such as the Galaxy Watch7 and Watch8 running Wear OS 7.0 or later. Choi Jong-min, vice president of the Health Development Group in Samsung Electronics' MX Business, said, "Sleep apnea is a sign that is hard to notice in daily life."

Samsung Electronics' sleep apnea feature received software as a medical device (SaMD) approval from the MFDS in September 2023, U.S. FDA 'De Novo' authorization in February 2024 and approval from Brazil's ANVISA in 2025, and it is now available in 84 countries worldwide.

blocks.cap: Photo: illustration, Getty Images

blocks.x: HHS is rolling back several health IT certification requirements, including certain AI transparency regulations. The HTI-5 final rule from ONC removes 14 of the 60 certification criteria in effect and revises seven more; most changes take effect on December 28, 2026, and ONC expects more than $1.5 billion in regulatory cost savings.

The rule removes requirements for developers to provide source attributions for AI recommendations in evidence-based and predictive decision support interventions, along with intervention risk management requirements.

“Certification no longer guarantees access to information about a predictive tool’s intended use, training data, performance, or limitations,” said attorney Mel Soliz. She recommends that health leaders build their own disclosure, validation, and bias-testing requirements into AI procurement contracts rather than relying on federal certification.
The rule also eliminates the voluntary certification criteria for security tags used to shield sensitive health information, which Soliz calls one of the most disappointing changes for providers.

This retrospective cohort study examined Epic's In Basket Augmented Response Technology, which generates AI-drafted replies to patient portal messages, at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. It analyzed 983 154 first responses from 1542 clinicians to 272 091 patients between March 1, 2023, and May 15, 2025; enterprise-level deployment came in December 2024.
Response tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% increase in overall message turnaround time, while using the tool on a given message was associated with a 29.5% reduction in turnaround time.

Tool use was not associated with an overall reduction of after-hours messaging burden. It was linked to fewer after-hours responses for test results–related queries received during working hours, but more after-hours responses for messages received after hours.
The authors conclude the tool may reduce the barrier to responding to certain messages while not uniformly reducing burden.

MANTIS (methylation profiling and artificial neural networks for time-dependent individualized survival predictions) is a precision AI tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction, built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Overview of the neural network architecture and training.

blocks.x: It generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding current clinical indicators. It was validated in three independent clinical trial cohorts of 898 medulloblastoma patients.

blocks.cap: Fig. 5: A majority of patients with average-risk MB may benefit from lower CSI doses.

blocks.x: Extended to estimate individualized treatment effects, MANTIS identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage (P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes.

Stanford Medicine researchers built an AI-enabled model of immune system changes in pregnancy, creating “digital twins” of individual pregnant women’s immune systems for virtual drug testing. The study published online Oct. 21 in Science Advances.

The system, called SIMCO (simulated immune modeling of clinical outcomes), was trained on responses from a quarter of a billion cells and longitudinal data from 63 pregnancies, then used to evaluate nine drug regimens already known to be safe for pregnancy.

The winning combination was aspirin and lansoprazole. “In the digital twin system, these two drugs in combination had a large effect on the delay of labor, 15 times higher than aspirin alone,” said senior author Brice Gaudilliere. Folic acid was also found to delay immunological progression toward labor.
The combination delayed labor in an animal model, and the researchers obtained FDA approval to test it in a human clinical trial.

blocks.cap: healthcare technology interface with AI integration and medical icons

blocks.x: Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access. Credentials are not shared with Claude, and patients can revoke access at any time.
