Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans.

The company will limit athenaPatient MCP access to AI assistants that do not use patient information to train their models, said Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer. "Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," he said.

More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. Brient said the goal was not to create additional work for clinicians: "It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use."

blocks.cap: Two clinicians discuss brain scans displayed on computer monitors.

blocks.x: Mayo Clinic Platform launched an AI-enabled Clinical Decision Support (CDS) solution for Mayo Clinic clinicians and organizations in its healthcare provider programs. It can be integrated into a growing number of EHR environments, so clinicians need not navigate several separate resources.

Beginning in November 2026, participating clinicians get a specialty-specific chat powered by a large language model, covering more than 35 specialties, citing peer-reviewed literature and updated daily, plus 22 clinical calculators accessible via chat or voice dictation, including proprietary Mayo calculators.
Chief operating officer Maneesh Goyal says the aim is less time searching and more time on patient care; chief medical officer Gelareh Zadeh stresses the tool does not replace clinical judgment.
Google, with health experts Dr. Elizabeth McGlynn and Dr. Dana Gelb Safran, published a whitepaper describing an end-to-end approach for evaluating AI use cases that address people's health needs.
The framework assesses models on accuracy, safety and usefulness, combining closed-question benchmarks, autoraters and expert human review across common and high-risk health scenarios.

blocks.cap: A healthcare worker in green scrubs looks at a smartphone held by a patient in a clinical office.

blocks.x: Google says it built and still uses the framework to check its own models, and shares the methodology to promote transparency and help developers, researchers and clinicians build AI tools people can trust.

This quality improvement study evaluated a fusion multimodal model with natural language processing that stratifies delirium risk for patients 60 or older admitted to non-ICU units, deployed live at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH) and externally validated at Mount Sinai Morningside (MSM) from December 2024 to December 2025.

The sample covered 33,095 admissions; 9,020 MSM admissions were scored during live operations and compared with 21,186 scored MSH admissions. The two patient populations differed in age, sex, race and ethnicity, diagnosis type, length of stay and dementia prevalence.

Without retraining, the model's AUROC was 0.91 at MSM and 0.94 at MSH, with positive predictive values of 25.9% and 19.4%. At MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate rose from 9.23% to 19.59% after deployment.
The authors conclude the model kept acceptable discrimination at the external site and increased diagnostic yield, but with a high false positive rate.

In this NEJM AI perspective, Dan Zeltzer, Tyler Tam, Benji Bhattacharya, Victoria Udalova and Maria Polyakova examine physical limits to AI substitution across physician specialties and what they imply for the physician workforce.

blocks.cap: Share of payments by specialty: physical (not substitutable by software-based AI), E&M, and nonphysical (potentially substitutable).

blocks.x: Across all 56 specialties (US$44.9bn in payments), 24% of payments are for physical services, 55% for evaluation and management, and 21% for nonphysical services potentially substitutable by AI.
Exposure varies widely: nonphysical work makes up 99% of pathology and 96% of diagnostic radiology payments, while physical services account for 68% in dermatology and 53% in orthopedic surgery.

GE HealthCare (GEHC) is introducing two AI-based capabilities for its Vscan Air handheld ultrasound system: Lung Guidance, which helps clinicians acquire lung ultrasound images, and AutoAS, which assesses for moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis.

Lung Guidance provides real-time guidance to correct anatomical landmarks across the standard eight-zone lung protocol, automatically captures clips when image-quality criteria are met, and supports B-line detection and scoring, according to the vendor. In validation testing, nonexpert users acquired diagnostic-quality exams 95.2% of the time, compared with 96.8% for expert users, GEHC said.
AutoAS analyzes at least two standard 2D echocardiographic views acquired with Vscan Air SL and indicates whether findings suggest moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis, along with a confidence score.

Both tools have received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance and carry the CE Mark. Existing Vscan Air customers with a valid Innovation Package subscription or license are expected to receive the updates by the end of November, GEHC said.

Safe deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography (NCCT) demands high sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) across common and uncommon findings requiring clinical attention. Here, we present a collaborative safety net integrating BrainCT-CLIP, a generalist foundation model via contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), with commercial detectors. Every examination remained in the reporting workflow, deprioritized only when no model returned a positive result.

In a retrospective multicenter external validation of consecutive emergency and trauma cohorts (n = 2001), standalone commercial detectors left 31 of 324 remarkable examinations deprioritized, including 16 target-disease false negatives and 15 outside their indications. In contrast, the collaborative system recovered every remarkable examination at a threshold prespecified in the development cohort, achieving 100% sensitivity and NPV while deprioritizing 18% of examinations (368/2001; 95% CI, 17–20).
These findings support generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization under radiologist oversight, with high sensitivity for intracranial findings requiring clinical attention.

This cross-sectional study investigated characteristics and reporting of updates to artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning–based medical devices cleared through the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) pathway, using the public FDA 510(k) database through March 31, 2025.

The study included 163 unique devices that explicitly reported using AI/ML; most (89.0%) analyzed medical imaging data. Among these devices, 56 (34.4%) received at least 1 update to their AI/ML algorithm, with a median (IQR) time until first update of 1.8 (0.9-2.5) years.
Of the updated devices, 42 (75.0%) received at least 1 update that changed their usage compared with the previous version; 9 (16.1%) had updates that only improved performance.

Reporting was inconsistent: participant information was absent for 42.9% of updated devices and sample size for 26.8%, and 48 devices (85.7%) provided no information on clinical or organizational benefit in any entry related to their updates.
The authors call for standardized reporting and postdeployment monitoring, noting that the FDA Predetermined Change Control Plan lets developers prespecify some changes without a new submission.

A research team led by Professor Lee In-seok of the Department of Gastroenterology at The Catholic University of Korea Seoul St. Mary's Hospital said on the 4th that it has begun validating the usefulness of a mobile app that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze health checkup records, genomic information and wearable device data and show a person's risk of chronic kidney disease. The validation is part of the project ‘Development of super-gap technology for phenome data-based AI prediction and management of health risks across the life cycle,’ under the AI-based personalized care service convergence leading program supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP).

The team is linking and standardizing Electronic Medical Record and health checkup data from multiple medical institutions, and adding physical activity, sleep and eating-habit information collected through wearable devices and the app to genomic analysis data, to develop AI models that predict the risk of onset and progression of diseases including chronic kidney disease. The app combines multiple clinical variables, such as health checkups and genomic tests, to calculate each person's absolute risk, and adds activity, sleep and heart rate data received from a Galaxy Watch. This process runs on the AI patient health platform (PHAIR), and in addition to chronic kidney disease risk, the app also provides life coaching.

The team also applied Federated Learning, a technique that lets several hospitals train AI together without directly sharing patient data. Clinical validation began in October 2026. The study recruits 50 people to use the app and a wearable for 3 months, and at month 3, kidney function (eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate) is checked with chest imaging and follow-up blood tests.

The full study period is 6 months, and the team plans to assess the service's use, satisfaction and usefulness to examine whether it can be applied in daily life. The team explained that existing risk prediction models focus on calculating the likelihood of disease onset or progression from clinical information at a single point in time, which has limited how well predictions translate into actual health management. This is because continuously tracking individual risk factors and providing tailored feedback requires an ongoing investment of clinicians' time and staff.

The team aims to link AI-calculated disease risk with app-based personalized lifestyle coaching, and to build a management system that continuously reflects changes in a person's health status and habits to help improve risk factors and prevent disease. Roles are also divided.

Seoul St. Mary's Hospital provides health checkup and clinical information, and the Department of Medical Informatics at The Catholic University of Korea is responsible for developing AI models that predict the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) and lung cancer. DigitalPharm handles AI analysis and platform operation, and Pyunghwa IS handles hospital information system operation and data conversion and transmission. The team expects AI technology that reflects Koreans' health characteristics to be meaningful in identifying high-risk groups early and providing individualized care before onset and worsening, and to contribute to advancing precision medicine and strengthening the competitiveness of future medical technology. Professor Lee In-seok said, “This study checks in a real clinical setting whether AI and wearables can solve the continuous risk management and feedback that were hard to achieve through outpatient care alone.” Led by Seoul St. Mary's Hospital, the project's participants include Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, the Sungkyun Institute of Bio-Convergence Science and Technology, WAYCEN, Samsung Electronics, NAVER Cloud, Miso Info Tech, Macrogen and DigitalPharm.

blocks.cap: Mobile Health Unit used in the RURAL study - American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 Abstract Poster MDP2290.

blocks.x: Artificial intelligence (AI) helped health professionals with no ultrasound experience in capturing quality heart scans in rural communities, which were then reviewed by off-site experts, according to new preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

In heart scans for 4,597 volunteer participants in the RURAL study, 98% of the scans included all six standard echocardiography views. Studies were rated adequate by the core laboratory experts more than 99% of the time. Scans were performed within a 15-minute target window 81% of the time, with a median time of 9.5 minutes.

Critical results were identified in 133 scans; 99% were returned to participants within three days. Fourteen non-sonographers (nurses, nursing assistants and CT technicians) completed the 2-hour training in AI-guided ultrasound.

“With real-time AI guidance and a rigorous quality-control system behind it, a nurse or CT technologist in a mobile unit can produce heart images good enough for research and good enough to flag serious heart problems that need follow-up,” said study author Sanjana Ravi, M.D., of the Duke University School of Medicine.
There was no direct comparison between sonographer-acquired images and those from AI-guided non-sonographers, and only one brand of software was used.

This 2-group randomized clinical trial enrolled 400 English-speaking pregnant or postpartum participants (infant younger than 6 months) from racial and ethnic minoritized groups, recruited online across 49 US states and the District of Columbia between October 2023 and December 2024.

Participants were randomized 1:1 to a generative AI maternal health chatbot or an active control of monthly children's books. Primary outcomes were anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-9) at 12 months.

The chatbot was not associated with differences in anxiety (adjusted mean difference, 0.10; 95% CI, −0.77 to 0.96) or depression (−0.23; 95% CI, −1.05 to 0.59), nor with emergency department visits, postpartum care, contraception use or sleep duration.

Among those pregnant at enrollment, the chatbot was associated with more self-reported pregnancy-related complications in the secondary 12-month analysis, but not in longitudinal analyses. The authors say secondary and exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously (NCT06053515).

San Jose, California-based Evident Vascular says the regulatory win applies to its Guidance System and Evident peripheral imaging catheters. They're intended for examination of pathology during certain peripheral vascular procedures handled by radiologists and other docs.

Evident says the system is designed to improve the clinician experience by combining high-fidelity imaging, “purpose-built AI,” and simple workflows without disruptions. Features include flush-less plug-and-play catheters, an “intuitive” user interface, and hands-free voice controls.

“FDA clearance marks an important milestone for Evident and the physicians who believed in this platform from our company's inception,” Howard Rosen, CEO and co-founder of Evident Vascular, said in a statement Nov. 4. “We engineered the entire imaging architecture to deliver the image fidelity physicians need in a system that is both intuitive and easy to use.”

Evident said its system integrates broad frequency bandwidth, advanced transducer design and advanced signal processing. It pairs custom imaging electronics with real-time processing, harnessing NVIDIA accelerated computing. AI is integrated into the imaging system and gathers user data to help improve the experience, according to the company. Evident said it plans to introduce further AI capabilities to further enhance exams and workflows.

AI scribes have been linked to lower documentation burden and faster note closure, but their equity impact is poorly studied. Researchers at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School examined same-day note closure across encounter types defined by patient language preference and interpreter use.

The cross-sectional study covered in-person adult primary care encounters at 14 clinics in Boston from May 2025 to May 2026: 209,009 encounters, 117,121 patients and 286 clinicians, who chose whether to use the scribe for each encounter.

After adjustment, AI scribe use was associated with higher same-day note closure for non-English-preference, language-concordant encounters (10.2 percentage points) and English-concordant encounters (1.7 percentage points). Results for interpreter-mediated and no-interpreter encounters were inconclusive because of wide confidence intervals.

The authors suggest lower scribe performance in complex conversations, such as those with multiple speakers or language switching, may explain the interpreter findings, and call for investment in bilingual workforce development and better support for interpreter-mediated workflows.

blocks.cap: Wrist-worn devices can provide useful information about people's ability to use their arms during stroke rehab. voronaman / Shutterstock

blocks.x: After a stroke, clinical tests used to track arm recovery are time-consuming, often cannot detect small changes, and don't capture everyday arm use. A team of NIH-funded researchers led by Dr. Sunghoon Lee of the University of Massachusetts Amherst created the digital arm performance scale (DAPS), published in Science Translational Medicine on September 30, 2026.

Sixty-one people who had a stroke within six months and 75 healthy people wore wrist accelerometers for thousands of hours in total. The researchers used machine learning to relate everyday arm movements to performance on clinical tests.

DAPS tracked improvements in arm movement as well as the clinical tests did, and was similarly useful for 79 other patients who had a stroke more than six months before. It could even distinguish patients with the highest possible clinical score from people who never had a stroke, and in simulations of two previous trials it required far fewer participants.

A deep-learning AI model can predict long-term mortality by quantifying aortic valve fibrotic and calcific tissue from CT angiography (CTA) scans, according to a study published November 5 in JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging. The international, multicenter study included 1,674 patients who underwent CTA at nine sites for routine TAVR planning, led by Kajetan Grodecki, MD, PhD, of Cedars-Sinai Medical Center.
The nnU-Net-based system was trained on 468 patients and applied to an external test set of 1,206 patients from centers in Poland, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States.

blocks.cap: Comparison of deep learning segmentation (A) with quantitative histology (B), demonstrating excellent agreement between methods (C). JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging

blocks.x: The model completed tissue analysis in 1.35 minutes on average versus 7.2 minutes for expert readers, with excellent agreement against experts (r = 0.915) and histology (r = 0.909). Over a mean 4.1 years, 469 patients (40%) died. Patients with the highest fibrotic tissue volumes (>0.940 cm³) faced a 2-fold higher death risk, and those with dense calcific attenuation a 1.5-fold higher risk.

This quality improvement study evaluates whether activation steering changes an open-weights large language model's (LLM) responses to questions about treatment for depression. Inference-time activation steering alters model activations to shift behavior on a target dimension while remaining undetectable by the end user.

Using the open-source tool DS4, a single steering direction contrasting antidepressant medication with self-directed approaches (diet, exercise, meditation, dietary supplements) was applied to DeepSeek version 4 Flash. Responses to 12 depression-treatment advice scenarios were generated at 30 steering amplitudes plus an unsteered baseline and scored by an LLM rater validated against a blinded human expert.

The LLM-rated medication-vs-self-care balance declined by 0.32 per unit of steering amplitude, from 1.25 at the strongest medication steering to 0.92 without steering and 0.17 at the strongest self-care steering.

blocks.cap: Outcomes of attention steering on medication and self-care content of depression treatment advice

blocks.x: Among scenarios without stated treatment preference, steering shifted medication extent most substantially (β = −0.44 per unit amplitude). A recommendation to consult a clinician was present in 322 of 372 responses (87%) and did not vary by steering amplitude.

The impact was dependent on patient preference: it did not override an explicit request for or against medication but impacted users without stated preference, who may be most susceptible to framing. The results suggest the need for independent auditing and benchmarking if models are used to inform clinical decisions.

In this retrospective cohort study of adults with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at Stanford Health Care (January 2019 to May 2025), a large language model pathway (GPT 5.0) was used to identify treat-to-target strategies and reasons for lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) nonescalation in clinical notes.

A total of 28,113 patients met the inclusion criteria, of whom 13,810 (49.1%) had above-goal LDL-C. The inference set comprised 14,785 notes from 13,394 patients, including 13,354 relevant visit notes.

A treat-to-target strategy was documented in 28.1% of relevant notes, most often an LDL-C target below 70 mg/dL (17.1%). LLT was not escalated in 11,842 notes (88.7%). Of these notes, 4,788 (40.4%) had at least 1 documented reason, most commonly patient-reported adverse effects (12.6%), LDL-C close to goal (6.9%), patient preference (6.8%), lifestyle changes (6.1%) and deferral to repeat labs (4.6%). Micro-weighted F1 scores ranged from 0.80 to 0.98.
Nearly 9 in 10 encounters with above-goal LDL-C did not escalate therapy; the authors suggest the findings could inform system-level digital health interventions.
Breast cancer treatment depends on histopathological features such as Nottingham grade and receptor-defined subtype, yet specialist pathologist access is limited where the workforce is scarce.

This single-center retrospective paired concordance study compared three flagship commercial multimodal LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.5) with a board-certified breast pathologist reference in 427 invasive breast cancers. Each model received the same overview and 16 H&E tissue tiles per case and the same prompt.

No model achieved agreement sufficient to support autonomous extraction of any feature. Gemini reported lymphovascular invasion in 26 packets, none supported by the images. Invasive carcinoma was absent from five packets, yet a Nottingham grade was returned in 14 of 15 model-case pairs. Claude ranked highest by raw histological-type concordance (87.4%) yet classified every lobular and micropapillary carcinoma as no-special-type. Model agreement with the report for grade (0.27–0.42) overlapped with that of a second pathologist (0.36).
Under the same prompt, each model showed a systematic error direction, including positive calls for findings absent from the input. The findings do not support autonomous use.
Deep Reasoning AI has received FDA 510(k) clearance (K262134) for NeuroDR, AI software for neurovascular CT angiography, 105 days after submission.

NeuroDR strips away soft tissue, bone and veins from head-and-neck CTA scans and produces 3D maximum intensity projections, curved planar reformats and volume renderings of the left and right internal carotid and vertebral arteries, with anterior and posterior circulations shown in separate displays.
It operates automatically in the background after a scan finishes and delivers the visualisations directly into hospital PACS as DICOM images.
It was created alongside post-processing provider 3DR Labs, which conducted the performance studies, and regulatory consultancy Innolitics, which handled the FDA pathway.

Korean researchers have developed a urine-testing technique that uses AI to distinguish between interstitial cystitis, overactive bladder and healthy individuals with up to 92 percent accuracy, potentially helping physicians differentiate between conditions with overlapping symptoms.

Asan Medical Center (AMC) said Tuesday that a team led by Professor Kim Jun-ki of the hospital’s Department of Convergence Medicine and Professor Shin Jung-hyun of the Department of Urology at Ewha Womans University Mokdong Hospital developed the technique by combining highly sensitive molecular detection with artificial intelligence.

The researchers combined surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) with AI. The team fabricated a SERS chip incorporating gold and zinc oxide nanostructures and analyzed urine samples of approximately 5 microliters each from 181 participants: 117 healthy controls, 19 patients with interstitial cystitis and 45 with overactive bladder.

Applying four machine learning methods (PCA-PLS-DA, PCA-LDA, XGBoost and LightGBM), the models distinguished among the three groups with up to 92 percent accuracy. The findings were published as a cover article in ACS Sensors; the team plans to validate the technique in larger patient groups.

Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. The researchers developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Overview of the gait foundation model, data acquisition and training pipeline.

blocks.x: Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearson's r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area (r = 0.83), and significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use.

blocks.cap: Fig. 5: Gait embeddings improve prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use beyond demographic and anthropometric baselines.

blocks.x: Leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. The authors say the findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal.

blocks.cap: Cleo Skin (Photo: Primaa)

blocks.x: The FDA has granted Breakthrough Device Designation to Cleo Skin, an artificial intelligence solution developed by Primaa to assist pathologists in diagnosing skin cancers from digitized biopsy slides and excised tissues.

Cleo Skin is the first AI tool in dermatopathology to hold both CE-IVDR certification in Europe, received in March 2026, and FDA Breakthrough Device Designation. The designation does not constitute US marketing authorization.

The tool analyzes whole slide images to flag areas suspicious for melanoma, offer indicative lesion classifications—including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and nevus—and suggest measurements such as margins, Breslow thickness, and mitotic regions. It supports rather than replaces pathologist evaluation.

In the SkinPerf2026 study, 16 pathologists across 11 French institutions evaluated 313 whole slide images; Cleo Skin improved overall melanoma sensitivity from 83.8% to 88.6%, and from 79.7% to 88.2% among junior pathologists. In an exploratory US study with PathPresenter, seven pathologists reviewed 75 slides, showing a 20% reduction in analysis time and a 17% gain in sensitivity among junior pathologists.

blocks.cap: AI-generated image

blocks.x: The 'AI-assisted drug review system' pursued by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) is set to be officially unveiled in early December. The agency had originally planned a briefing for the pharmaceutical industry early this month, but after further strengthening internal validation to improve the system's completeness, it will unveil the system to coincide with a ceremony celebrating the success of the AI project.

According to the MFDS's food and drug AI transformation TF (headed by Kim Ik-sang), a pilot run is currently under way, centered on internal reviewers. LG AI Research took part in building the system, which stands out for having been trained specifically for drug review work.

It will first support reviews in new drug quality and bioequivalence (bioavailability and equivalence), and verify pre-review checklists for product approval reviews. The MFDS plans to expand its scope to reviews of safety and efficacy data and other areas.

Global regulators are actively exploring AI adoption, with the U.S. FDA introducing 'Elsa,' a generative AI platform for all staff. The MFDS completed the system less than a year after setting up the TF in January.
Private patient information was improperly used in recent radiology artificial intelligence research, according to an alert from Weill Cornell Medicine shared on Thursday.

The institution says it first found out about the incident on Sept. 6, immediately launching an investigation. It learned that unnamed individuals entered patient info from Weill Cornell Imaging at NewYork-Presbyterian and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital into AI tools for processing using machine learning, without patient permission and in violation of its privacy policies.

The information included medical record and radiology accession numbers, dates, times of service, facility and healthcare provider names, plus clinical information such as diagnoses, treatment plans and procedural histories. Patients' names, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers and financial details were not disclosed.

Weill Cornell said it has not found evidence that unauthorized individuals accessed the information and there is no indication it was misused. It has suspended the research activity, requested that all involved data be deleted, and is providing additional staff education on the appropriate use of AI. It did not disclose who misused the data nor the focus of the research.

blocks.cap: Technology will be able to detect diabetes and eventually heart disease in routine eye tests

blocks.x: AI will be used in routine eye scans as part of a scheme to detect early signs of illnesses such as heart disease and diabetes.

The Northern Ophthalmic Research and Innovation (NORI) hub at Sunderland University has received £12.2m from the government through UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for the project in the hope of diagnosing patients quicker.
Matthew Campbell, interim pro vice-chancellor for health and co-director of NORI, said the money would help the team develop the technology and take it into international markets.
While the tool will initially focus on diabetes and cardiovascular disease, the approach could later be expanded to dementia and strokes.
NORI is one of five new UKRI-backed healthcare hubs using technology to diagnose illnesses.
Science minister Chris McDonald, who visited NORI on Thursday, said: "Earlier diagnosis means better outcomes for patients and less pressure on our NHS, and technology has a vital role to play."

The technology will use the tiny blood vessels and nerve tissue at the back of the eye, which NORI said can reveal clues about a person's wider health before symptoms appear. AI will be used to analyse the routine eye scans alongside NHS health records and community data to identify subtle changes which may signal early signs of disease.

Campbell said: "This investment creates a new health innovation ecosystem for the North East. We now have the scale to develop technologies, test them in real-world healthcare settings and take them into national and international markets."

blocks.x: In the largest study of its kind, researchers analyzed heart MRI scans from 27,382 patients undergoing investigation for known or suspected heart conditions in the U.K. and United States, comparing AI-derived and clinician-derived measurements of left-ventricular ejection fraction.

Patients were followed for an average of more than five years (median 5.6 years), during which 3,458 deaths occurred. AI ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 57,936 vs 58,097) and marginally better discrimination (C index 0.669 vs 0.637) for all-cause mortality; after adjustment for age and sex the advantage remained but was smaller (C index 0.781 vs 0.777).
The AI tool analyzed scans in approximately 2–3 seconds per patient. This compared to previous work by the team that found expert clinician analysis typically takes around 13 minutes.

The research was led by City St George's, University of London and University College London, and published in The Lancet Digital Health. The authors say the findings support AI for first-line ejection-fraction measurement with clinician oversight, to be tested in prospective studies.

blocks.x: AI-generated interpretations of echocardiograms were comparable in accuracy to preliminary interpretations prepared by sonographers and cardiologists, and reduced the time cardiologists spent interpreting each scan almost by half, according to preliminary late-breaking science presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

Researchers say this is the first randomized trial testing an AI tool to craft a full echocardiogram report. An AI tool, a sonographer and a cardiologist each prepared preliminary reports for the same 1,200 echocardiograms; cardiologists then finalized them without knowing who made the first draft.

Cardiologists made substantial changes to 50.6% of the AI-generated preliminary interpretations, compared with 49.7% of those prepared by sonographers and cardiologists — meeting the criteria for non-inferiority. They spent an average of 4.6 minutes per echocardiogram on AI drafts versus 8.5 minutes without AI assistance, a time savings of about 46%.

“AI cannot, however, replace the human team,” said co-senior author Keane K. Lee, M.D., M.S., of Kaiser Permanente. The study, across 21 Kaiser Permanente Northern California medical centers, is a research abstract that is not peer-reviewed.

Post-traumatic stress disorder affects numerous trauma survivors after emergency department discharge, yet emergency clinicians face severe time constraints that make existing screening tools impractical.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Schematic overview of PREVIA.

blocks.x: Researchers from NYU Langone Health introduce PREVIA, a clinically-informed large language model ensemble that predicts PTSD risk from unstructured patient trauma narratives given in response to a routine-care question in the ED — “What brought you to the ED?” — by extracting early post-traumatic stress symptoms, peri-traumatic symptoms, risk and protective factors.

Among N = 145 patients at two New York City level-1 trauma centers, enrolled within 24 hours of trauma and assessed for PTSD one month later, PREVIA forecast PTSD with AUROC = 78.49% and sensitivity = 95.4%. On 30 randomly selected patients it performed comparably to an emergency clinician specialized in PTSD (PREVIA: AUROC = 84.39%, sensitivity = 100.00%; clinician: AUROC = 83.86%, sensitivity = 88.89%).

blocks.cap: Fig. 4: Example application of PREVIA’s three-layer LLM ensemble to a synthetic ED trauma narrative: PTSD case.

blocks.x: PREVIA also generates interpretable explanations without additional clinical burden; the authors say the findings warrant validation in larger, independent cohorts.
Multiple teams participating in ARPA-H’s Advocate program have already had an initial informational meeting with the FDA, less than two months after the clinical AI program launched.
The teams aim to submit autonomous AI heart failure devices within two years, program manager Haider Warraich said.

blocks.x: Hospitals collectively lost an estimated $132 billion last year to write-offs for bad debt and final claim denials, according to a new report from revenue cycle analytics company Kodiak Solutions — up nearly 18% from 2024, with write-offs taking about 10 percent of net revenue.

The increase comes despite rising revenue cycle technology budgets, which grew 7.6% to $69 billion this year per Forrester, with more AI tools — including emerging agentic AI for tasks such as prior authorizations — promising to improve hospitals’ financial performance.

Kodiak researchers said providers may not be “adequately distinguishing between technology needed to operate the revenue cycle and the capabilities needed to optimize their financial performance.” A Peterson Health Technology Institute report found AI for prior authorization has yet to reduce costs systemwide, as payers and providers wage an AI arms race.

Cleerly presented primary results from PARAMOUNT, the first randomized trial of AI-QCT-guided care against usual care, as Late-Breaking Science at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. Compared with usual care based on stress testing, care guided by AI-based quantitative coronary CT analysis (AI-QCT) improved diagnostic certainty and led to more patients receiving lipid-lowering therapy.

Between January 2025 and February 2026, 530 participants at 21 sites with suspected coronary artery disease and elevated LDL-C (≥100 mg/dL) were randomized. Preliminary results are based on 523 participants; women made up 57% of participants.

“PARAMOUNT shows that when we measure plaque directly and use it to guide care, physicians gain clearer answers and patients are far more likely to start preventive therapy,” said co-principal investigator Todd C. Villines, MD. Plaque-based care resulted in significantly fewer patients without obstructive CAD among those referred to the cath lab and did not increase overall rates of catheterizations or revascularizations.
The results have not yet been peer reviewed and should be considered preliminary; full results are expected to be published in early 2027.

A smartphone-based artificial intelligence (AI) voice analysis system can detect worsening heart failure symptoms more than three weeks early, significantly outperforming the standard of care, according to late-breaking DETECT-HF trial data presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 and published in JACC: Heart Failure.

DETECT-HF evaluated Cordio Medical's HearO system in 563 ambulatory heart failure patients. It predicted more than 70% of significant heart failure events an average of 24.6 days in advance. Conventional daily weight measurements have a sensitivity of approximately 20%, according to lead investigator William T. Abraham, MD.

HearO collects six standardized spoken sentences each day and evaluates intonation, breathing patterns and other acoustic features. AI algorithms build a patient-specific voice model and alert clinicians when patterns of worsening heart failure appear.

Participants completed 85% of scheduled recordings; the unexplained alert rate was 2.65 per patient per year, and no device-related adverse events were reported. HearO received FDA breakthrough device designation, and the company hopes to launch in the U.S. in 2027.

Large language models can perform on par with radiologists when it comes to selecting the most appropriate MRI protocols for patients, according to a new analysis. The findings suggest certain models could help standardize MRI protocol selection, which is typically done manually.

Researchers led by Dr. Zeynep Bendella of University Hospital Bonn evaluated four open-weight LLMs using 1,200 consecutive MRI referral forms, with a consensus of two board-certified radiologists as the reference standard.

GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 each earned 94% protocol accuracy. MedGemma-27B-Text-IT achieved 79%, and Gemma-3-27B-IT had the lowest performance, with 58%. Unacceptable selections were 5.8% for GPT-OSS and 5.9% for Qwen3, versus 24.7% for MedGemma and 68.3% for Gemma3.

The most common error was choosing a protocol that was anatomically appropriate but clinically suboptimal. The authors cautioned that the variation in outputs and frequency of unacceptable selections highlight the risks of relying on automated recommendations without clinical oversight.

Radiotherapy is a pivotal treatment for active, moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease (TED), but responses vary, and the clinical activity score (CAS) has limited predictive value. The authors built a multi-sequence model integrating clinical data, conventional imaging and MRI radiomic features to predict radiotherapy response.

85 TED subjects treated with standardized radiotherapy (20 Gy) were retrospectively enrolled. Radiomic features from extraocular muscles on T1CE and T2WI MRI were used to develop models with nine machine learning algorithms.

Among 85 patients, 46 were responders and 39 non-responders. Clinical models showed limited performance (AUC = 0.700), whereas T1CE, T2WI and multi-sequence radiomics reached AUCs of 0.850, 0.875 and 0.933. The integrated model achieved the highest AUC (0.942) and significantly outperformed the clinical model (P = 0.040).

The model helps guide individualized decision-making, reduce ineffective radiotherapy, and advance personalized management for thyroid eye disease, supporting individualized risk stratification after prospective validation.

blocks.x: The Food and Drug Administration on Friday issued a discussion paper on robotic medical devices with autonomous or remote teleoperation capabilities and is requesting feedback on the systems’ benefits and risks. Comments are due Jan. 5; a public workshop is scheduled for Dec. 2-3.

In the U.S., no remotely teleoperated or fully autonomous robotic devices have received marketing authorization as of July, the FDA said. In October, Dr. Vipul Patel performed a robotic prostatectomy on a patient about 35 miles away under an investigational device exemption.

Manufacturers are also exploring autonomous functions, which could include obtaining a blood draw without a phlebotomist and finding or stopping life-threatening bleeding inside the body. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning and connectivity are driving expansion of robotic applications, the FDA said.

Autonomy could support procedural accuracy, reproducibility or workflow efficiency, but distinct risks such as incorrect autonomous execution, reduced user vigilance and limited adaptability to procedural variability may accompany the benefits.
New findings demonstrate AI’s aptitude for identifying technical flaws in studies where medical decisions are on the line.

The study, a medRxiv preprint titled “Large language models detect methodological errors that human peer review misses in clinical trials,” revisited an earlier experiment in which errors were inserted into three reports of randomized clinical trials; untrained human reviewers achieved a mean major-error detection score of 27%.

Fifteen large language models, including four open-weight models, were tested on the same errors. Their major-error detection scores ranged from 53% to 96%. To reduce the risk of memorization, the test was repeated on three clinical trials published in 2026, where scores ranged from 51% to 99%, and from 66% to 87% for the open-weight models.

The models still flagged 2% to 29% of the error types in control reports without inserted errors, most often conclusions not supported by the results. Opus 5.5 achieved the highest major-error detection score (99%), while GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna scored 92% and 87%. The authors suggest that relying on human peer review alone may leave avoidable methodological errors undetected.
The new tool checks clinicians’ questions for privacy concerns and chatbots’ answers for accuracy.

MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, on Wednesday launched CrossCover, a tool the company said is meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots while preserving patient and provider privacy.

Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. “We can take away some of the challenges and risks and problems with the technology so that physicians can feel more confident in using it,” he said.

CrossCover takes an approach that contradicts that of medical AI tools from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and electronic health record company Epic, which are trying to incorporate an ever-widening repertoire of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. Rather than requiring clinicians to register with their national identification numbers or brokering privacy agreements, MDCalc’s tool focuses on stripping out those types of information from clinicians’ queries.

No evidence-based guidance exists for triaging individuals with positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) tests for rheumatology referral. The researchers developed and deployed an interpretable clinical prediction model, AURA (AUtoimmune Risk Assessment), to predict which individuals with incident positive ANA tests will develop systemic autoimmune disease, and evaluated it in a 2-year randomized pragmatic study.

The model was integrated into the electronic health record at a single academic health system. ANA-positive individuals were randomly assigned 1:1; in the intervention group, those with high-risk scores were invited for expedited rheumatology evaluation, while in the control group risk scores were calculated but not acted on.

Of 2385 randomly assigned individuals, 954 were analyzed in the intervention group and 1006 in the control group. The intervention group had a significantly shorter time to autoimmune disease diagnosis (hazard ratio, 1.9; 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.7; P<0.001); median time to diagnosis was 43 days versus 138 days.
Among those evaluated by rheumatology within 6 months, 23% in the intervention group and 16% in the control group were diagnosed with an autoimmune disease (P=0.07).
Researchers will present their experience in rolling out 11 triage AI algorithms across three hospitals (Thursday, December 3 | 9:30 a.m.-10:30 a.m. | R3-SSIN07-1 | Room E450B).

Real-world evidence on large-scale AI deployment in clinical practice remains limited, noted presenter Domenico Mastrodicasa, MD, of the University of Washington, and colleagues. The group evaluated how system-wide implementation of multiple AI triage tools affected report turnaround time at a quaternary academic health system that includes a Level 1 trauma center.

The algorithms were deployed in stages between September 2023 and August 2025 and processed more than 742,000 imaging exams. The researchers compared median turnaround times before and after deployment.

The largest gain came for endotracheal tube malposition, where turnaround time dropped by about 76%, followed by rib fracture (53%) and brain vessel occlusion (29%). Pulmonary embolism and intracranial hemorrhage, however, saw no improvement. The researchers say this likely reflects higher proportions of follow-up or inpatient studies with known findings.

“As imaging volumes increase, timely identification of clinically significant findings is becoming more challenging,” the authors wrote. “Our experience shows that system-wide implementation of AI triage tools can support radiologists by prioritizing critical findings and improving workflow efficiency in high-volume settings. Since performance varied across applications, realizing these benefits requires targeted deployment and ongoing optimization as clinical workflows evolve.”
Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) support affordable disease diagnosis. Machine learning (ML) can improve RDT interpretation but often relies on large, proprietary, and costly real-world image libraries.

We present SynSight – a ML-enabled RDT segmentation and classification pipeline trained on synthetic data. Validated on HIV (98% sensitivity, 99% specificity) and COVID-19 RDTs (up to 99% accuracy), SynSight enables rapid ML training without real-world training images, keeping pace with new RDT development.

Google launched Tuesday Gemini for healthcare, an agentic artificial intelligence platform aimed at connecting complex clinical, financial and administrative workflows used by healthcare providers and payers. It was developed alongside clinical and health plan leaders and is built to support HIPAA compliance.

“The fundamental challenge in healthcare isn't a lack of information—it's the immense friction of making that data actionable across a highly regulated ecosystem,” said Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud CEO.

The “integrated, fully governed” system has four main components: skills for healthcare work, connectors to administrative systems, an open healthcare partner ecosystem and a secure, governed platform with open model choice. It integrates with EHRs, billing systems, clinical guidelines, coding and CMS datasets.

Gemini for healthcare is available in preview as of Nov. 10 to Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus customers. Partners include GoodRx, Epic, IMO Health, Oracle Health, Infinitus and Suki; health systems HCA Healthcare and Northwell Health have also teamed up with Google for the launch.
HCA's Michael Schlosser, M.D., said the company is “exploring how Gemini can interpret and synthesize complex patient information from multiple electronic health record systems and care settings.”

This cross-sectional study examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical trials conducted starting in 2022. Researchers analyzed interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, with start dates from January 2022 onward, to characterize how AI use is planned and described.

Of 8559 records returned by the search, the final cohort comprised 1212 interventional trials. Planned generative AI use, including large language models, rose sharply, from no trials starting in 2022 to 100 of 491 (20.4%) of those starting in 2025. Eight trials planned for use of AI agents for patient follow-up or health education delivery, among other purposes.

blocks.cap: Bar Graphs of Characteristics of Included Trials

blocks.x: The most common clinical conditions were cancer (20.0%), neurological and mental health (19.6%), and cardiovascular and metabolic disease (18.6%). AI was most often used for screening and predictive modeling of disease risk or treatment selection (39.8%). The United States accounted for 303 trials (25.0%) and China for 149 (12.3%).

Because ClinicalTrials.gov has no structured AI fields or reporting requirements, method details were often absent; the authors say structured registry fields aligned with AI reporting standards would improve transparency.

Persistent fever after initiating intravenous antibiotics is common in hospitalized patients with cancer and often leads to additional imaging and antimicrobial escalation. The researchers developed and externally validated machine learning models to predict persistent fever 48–72 h after antibiotic initiation using electronic health records from two academic hospitals.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Flow diagram illustrating the cohort extraction steps for the UME and BWH datasets.

blocks.x: Final cohorts comprised 987 hospital stays at University Medicine Essen (UME) and 7409 hospital stays at Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH). The best-performing model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.79–0.84) internally and 0.78 (95% CI 0.77–0.79) externally. Temperature-related variables were the dominant predictors.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: Discrimination, clinical utility, and calibration of prediction models in the internal (UME) and external (BWH) validation cohorts.

blocks.x: Approximately one quarter of antibiotic escalations and chest CT scans occurred in patients correctly predicted not to remain febrile. Clinical use should be limited to an adjunctive role rather than standalone rule-out decision-making, and prospective studies are required.

Pharmaceutical advertising and drug recommendations by consumer-facing artificial intelligence: a controlled study — Mahmud Omar, Reem Agbareia, Jolion McGreevy, Alexis Zebrowski, Ashwin Ramaswamy, Michael A Gorin, Esther-Maria Antao, Benjamin S Glicksberg, Ankit Sakhuja, Alexander W Charney, Eyal Klang, Girish N Nadkarni.

Advertising shifted treatment selection by LLMs towards the promoted drug. Guideline concordance remained high, meaning that shifts among guideline-concordant treatments could evade evaluations of treatment correctness.
The influence of advertising was often undisclosed. Whether these output shifts could affect prescribing or patient decisions requires direct study.

Increasingly, physicians must oversee AI systems to detect system malfunctions. We studied 48 physicians in a randomized controlled study using an increasingly malfunctioning AI for cardiac auscultation. Diagnostic performance declined alongside AI reliability, even when physicians were cognitively forced to make an initial classification, and when human performance exceeded AI reliability. Physicians’ confidence declined faster than their trust in AI.

Forty-eight physicians were randomly assigned to an AI-First or AI-Second condition and classified 40 recorded heart sounds as normal or abnormal. To simulate malfunction, system reliability declined stepwise across four blocks (90%, 60%, 50%, 0%).

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Study results.

blocks.x: AI-assisted diagnostic performance declined from 81.45% to 58.33%. Under low system reliability, combined human-AI performance fell below the unassisted human baseline, and only 12.5% of participants reported noticing declining system reliability.

The authors say effective oversight may require action at the system and organizational levels, such as uncertainty indicators or explanations, with accountability shared with AI deployers and providers.

blocks.x: Samsung Medical Center is teaming up with Heidi, a global healthcare artificial intelligence (AI) company, to introduce AI technology that converts speech generated during patient consultations into text.
Samsung Medical Center said on the 13th that it signed a business agreement with Heidi on the 12th to cooperate on medical AI services. The agreement is Heidi's first entry into Korea.

Under the agreement, the two sides will focus on applying speech-to-text technology to DARWIN, the hospital's own medical information system. They also plan to cooperate in areas such as telemedicine and appointment booking, building on the medical AI agent Heidi is developing.

Founded in 2019, Heidi develops AI technology that supports clinicians in their care work. It currently supports more than 3 million (300만건) consultations a week in 110 languages across 190 countries. Its main service is technology that converts speech generated during consultations into text. It also offers services for clinical settings, such as generating templates tailored to each specialty and supporting clinical decisions through real-time AI question answering.

Heidi CEO Thomas Kelly said, "Samsung Medical Center is Heidi's first case of entering Korea, and we plan to pursue collaboration with it as a key partner," adding, "We hope Korean hospitals, building on our technology, can further strengthen their medical capabilities while keeping their warm values toward patients."

Samsung Medical Center President Park Seung-woo said, "We expect this cooperation with Heidi to further speed up building a patient-friendly AI medical environment," adding, "It will be an occasion for an important leap toward realizing future medicine and shaping the tomorrow of smart hospitals."
Meanwhile, Samsung Medical Center ranked 4th in the world and 1st in Korea in the 'World's Best Smart Hospitals' ranking published by the U.S. weekly news magazine Newsweek.

In the healthcare IT maturity assessments of the U.S. Healthcare Information and Management Systems Society (HIMSS), it also achieved Stage 7, the highest level, in 4 areas: healthcare IT infrastructure (INFRAM), electronic medical record systems (EMRAM), digital imaging (DIAM) and healthcare data analytics (AMAM). In particular, it was the first in the world to receive Stage 7 certification in INFRAM and DIAM, in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

blocks.cap: The Ministry of Health and Welfare held a pilot opening ceremony on the 11th for the 'public healthcare AI highway', which connects Kangwon National University Hospital and Yeongwol Medical Center in real time (photo: Ministry of Health and Welfare).

blocks.x: Public hospitals in Gangwon are building a care system that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to link everything from patient transfers to surgery, discharge and referral back to the community. Starting with Kangwon National University Hospital and Yeongwol Medical Center, the government plans to extend medical AI to 72 public hospitals nationwide by 2029.

The government has built a system that delivers medical AI models validated by leading institutions such as Seoul National University Hospital to regional public hospitals through a dedicated high-speed network, national graphics processing unit (GPU) computing resources and a standard integration platform.

At the opening ceremony, 3 AI agents linked to electronic medical records (EMR) were demonstrated. The 'transfer referral and return letter summary and generation AI' is expected to cut the drafting of a transfer referral, which used to take more than 10 minutes, to under 1 minute. The 'pre-anesthesia assessment generation AI' and the 'discharge record summary and generation AI' also produce drafts, while the attending physician makes the final clinical judgment, edits the documents and signs them electronically.

The government will run pilot validation at 8 medical institutions and launch the main project in April 2027, expanding participation to up to 35 hospitals. Minister Jeong Eun-kyeong said, “The government will make 2026 the first year of healthcare AX.”
Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports and labs, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases.

Dyania trains its models with the Nvidia NeMo framework; inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The AI answered 88 questions per patient, and researchers used the dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years.

blocks.x: Physicians’ AI use is moving beyond administrative tasks to more everyday clinical decision support, like searching through medical literature, according to a survey published Thursday by Doximity. More than half of physicians said they use AI daily and another third use it at least once a week.

The Doximity survey of more than 3,300 of the firm’s U.S. doctors shows that the share of physicians using AI for clinical decision support nearly doubled to 63%, up from 37% in 2025. Also, more physicians — 70% from just over half in last year’s survey — are using AI to comb through troves of medical literature.

A majority (81%) of physicians said that using AI has taught them something they previously didn’t know, including updated guidelines, alternative diagnoses or treatment options. Another 65% said that AI tools have helped with developing their clinical skills and knowledge.

But 61% worry that trainees will rely on AI too much and not develop their own set of clinical skills. Nearly half were concerned about overreliance on AI, and three in four physicians said they encountered a factual inaccuracy at least once in the past year while using AI for work. Over a quarter said the effort they put into correcting or double-checking AI output has decreased compared with a year ago.
